x: Preface — Why This Book? They were nineteen per cent slower. They believed they were twenty per cent faster. Both numbers describe the same sixteen developers, in the same experiment, in the same week. — after METR, arXiv 2507.09089 A What you'll learn: Why the two most-cited numbers in this field contradict each other, and why that is the interesting part The evidence stance this book takes, and the four grades it uses Which layers of software engineering are dating in months and which have not dated in fifty years How to read this book if you are shipping on Monday, and how to read it if you intend to cite it The claim this preface defends: the disagreement about whether AI makes engineers faster is not a measurement problem to be resolved by better surveys. It is a structural fact about where the bottleneck moved, and it is the reason a new lifecycle is needed rather than a new tool.

Two figures dominate every argument about AI and software engineering. The first: 55.8% faster. A controlled experiment at GitHub and Microsoft Research put developers on a scoped task — implement an HTTP server in JavaScript — with and without an assistant. The assisted group finished in roughly half the time. The second: 19% slower. A randomised controlled trial run by METR took sixteen experienced open-source developers and gave them 246 real tasks in repositories they had contributed to for an average of five years. When AI tools were permitted, the tasks took nineteen per cent longer. Both studies are competent. Neither is fraudulent. They are cited by opposing camps as though only one can be true, and this is where the discourse fails, because both are true and the gap between them is the most informative object in the field. Notice what changes between the two experiments. Not the model — both used frontier tooling of their moment. Not the developers' competence — the METR participants were, if anything, more expert. What changed was the task: from a small greenfield problem with a clear specification and no existing code to respect, to a large brownfield problem where most of the work is discovering which of ten thousand existing decisions your change must not violate. Read Figure 0.1 as a warning about instruments rather than a verdict about tools. Every point on that line is a real measurement. The line slopes down. Any argument that quotes one point and omits the l

The bottleneck moved. Software engineering spent seventy years optimising the production of code. Compilers, high-level languages, libraries, frameworks, package managers, IDEs, continuous integration, containers — a long march of tools whose common purpose was to make correct code cheaper to write. The lifecycle we inherited, in all its variants, encodes that assumption. Requirements, design, implementation, test, release: a pipeline built around the premise that implementation is the expensive step. Implementation is no longer the expensive step. This is not a prediction; it is the plainest reading of the evidence, including the pessimistic evidence. Even METR's slowed-down developers were not slowed because generating code was hard. They were slowed by reviewing, correcting, and reconciling what was generated. This book's spine, stated once, plainly: SDLC assumed the bottleneck was producing code. ADLC assumes the bottleneck is verifying and directing it. Everything else follows from that sentence. If verification is the constraint, then the engineering discipline that matters is the design of the apparatus that verifies and directs — the specifications that state intent, the context that the model sees, the sensors that catch what it got wrong, the structure that limits what it can break, and the graph that tells it where things are. Code becomes something closer to a build output. The durable artefacts move up a layer. That is a claim about engineering. There is a second

Every empirical claim in this book carries a grade: Grade | Meaning | A | Peer-reviewed, randomised, or large-N empirical | B | Preprint with credible methodology, not yet reviewed | C | Analyst research — rigorous, partly proprietary, partly self-reported | D | Vendor or practitioner claim — useful signal, weak evidence | The grades are not decoration and they are not symmetric in what they permit. A D claim can motivate a practice; it cannot establish one. An A finding on sixteen developers still generalises only as far as sixteen developers. Two commitments follow, and I would rather be held to them than praised for them. The first: no selective citation. Where the evidence is mixed, all of it appears, including the parts that damage the argument. Chapter 4 presents the case that agent-assisted codebases accumulate persistent complexity while their velocity gains prove transient. That is not a friendly finding for a book proposing a lifecycle built on delegation, and it appears in full because a reader who discovers the counter-evidence elsewhere is entitled to conclude the author knew and hid it. The second: verified figures only. Writing this book involved checking the numbers in my own research notes against the primary sources. Nine of them were wrong. A churn statistic that had drifted from 5.5%→7.9% into 3.1%→5.7% somewhere in secondary coverage. A Gartner forecast that turned out to be two different forecasts fused into one. A benchmark score from a single-author pr

Two readers, and I refuse to choose between them. If you are shipping software. You are an engineering leader or a senior practitioner and you must decide what changes next quarter. You need instruments, not epistemology. The book gives you: the Autonomy Ladder (Chapter 13) for deciding how much authority to grant on which code, and why the answer is a function of structure and blast radius rather than enthusiasm; the metrics (Chapter 14) that tell you whether delegation is working, including the ones nobody currently measures; the maturity model (Chapter 15) so you can locate yourself honestly; the 90-day plan (Chapter 26); and the anti-patterns (Chapter 21), which is the chapter most readers will recognise themselves in and the one you should probably read first. If you intend to cite this. You are a researcher, and you need to know what is evidence, what is synthesis, and what is the author's proposal. The book keeps these separate on purpose. Where I am proposing rather than reporting — the metric families, the autonomy ladder, the maturity model, the reconciliation of the three preference instruments — I say so. Chapter 27 collects the open problems, and Chapter 10 contains an admission that the most elegant argument in the book rests on a mechanism with no causal evidence behind it yet. I would rather hand you a falsifiable claim than a persuasive one. The two readers need each other more than either would like. Industry practice in this field is currently running well

t: 0.5 How to read a book about a moving target
x: The obvious objection to this book is that it will be obsolete before it is read. Model checkpoints turn over in weeks. The configuration mechanisms described in Chapter 7 are, in the words of the researchers who catalogued them, "a point-in-time snapshot of a field whose conventions are still consolidating." The objection is correct about some layers and wrong about others, and the difference is the most useful thing in this preface. Taleb's Lindy effect says that for non-perishable things, life expectancy grows with age: an idea that has survived fifty years will probably outlive one that arrived last spring. Applied here it is a straightforward editorial instrument. Parnas published On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules in 1972. Fifty-four years later it is not merely still correct, it has acquired a second and unintended application: the information-hiding discipline that was designed to limit what a human must understand turns out to be the mechanism that limits what an agent can get wrong. That is a Lindy bet paying out. AGENTS.md is roughly eighteen months old. It may well become permanent infrastructure — Chapter 7 shows it converging bottom-up across tools and then being donated to a foundation, which is genuinely remarkable for the timescale — but you should hold the two beliefs with different grips. So: this book excludes benchmark leaderboards and model comparisons; dates every claim about a specific tool's capability, because those claims

Five parts. Part I — The Discontinuity establishes that something actually broke, using evidence rather than assertion. Chapter 1 resolves a naming collision that has made most of the existing literature on this subject unusable, and it should be read first. Chapter 2 identifies the single result that justifies treating any of this as engineering. Chapters 3 and 4 present the productivity and quality evidence in full, including the parts that argue against the book. Chapter 5 names which inherited assumptions fail. Part II — The Four Pillars is the engineering core: context, harness, graph, and structure, presented as nested rings of control rather than a list of techniques, plus verification and security running across all four. Part III — The Lifecycle assembles those pillars into a process model with two loops, an autonomy ladder, a metric system, a maturity model, and an argument about organisational shape. Part IV — The Human Transformation is the part I expect to be argued with, and the part that matters most. Ten shifts. The perception–reality inversion and how to defeat it. What delegating effort does to judgment. How to train juniors when the tasks they learned on are the tasks that automated first. Part V — Modes and Practice places vibe coding fairly, names the moment a prototype becomes a system, addresses the inversion that legacy codebases need this discipline most and can adopt it least, and closes with a 90-day plan and a list of things nobody has solved.

What I owe you: graded evidence, named sources, explicit separation of finding from proposal, and an honest account of what is unresolved. What I ask in return: read the parts that contradict your position. If you arrived believing this technology is transformative, Chapter 4 is for you. If you arrived believing it is overstated, Chapter 2 is for you. The interesting position is available only to readers who hold both. One more thing, and it is the sentence I would keep if I could keep only one. A harness cannot verify correctness against a requirement that was never articulated. Every control in this book — every sensor, every guide, every fitness function, every graph — operates on stated intent. Where intent is unstated, no apparatus helps, and the failure is silent, because generated code that satisfies an unstated requirement incorrectly looks exactly like generated code that satisfies it correctly. Specification is the last human monopoly. The rest of this book is about building the apparatus that makes that monopoly worth holding.
The bottleneck moved from producing code to verifying and directing it; every practice in this book is a consequence of that single relocation.

x: Somewhere between 2024 and 2026, two communities independently needed a name for something new, reached for the same four letters, and did not notice each other. The first community builds AI agents and sells them. Their problem is that the thing they ship behaves differently every time you talk to it. They needed a lifecycle for that, and they called it the Agent Development Lifecycle. The term appears to have been coined by Arthur around 2024 and was subsequently formalised by Salesforce as a five-phase Agentforce model, by IBM as a phased framework with iterative loops, and by Glean, EPAM, and Atlan in their own variants through 2025 and 2026 D. The second community builds ordinary software — payment systems, internal tools, data pipelines — but has replaced a large fraction of its typing with agents. Their problem is that code now arrives faster than anyone can read it. They needed a lifecycle for that, and they called it the Agentic Development Lifecycle. Cycode built a security platform around the term in March 2026; Forrester published The Agentic Development Security Tools Landscape in Q2 2026 — by Cycode's own account the first landscape Forrester had published for the category, "a market that didn't exist a year ago" D. Both communities abbreviate to ADLC. Both position it against SDLC. Both say, correctly, that SDLC assumed determinism and that this assumption has failed. t: 1.2 Meaning A — the agent is the product
x: In Meaning A, the agent is the thing you sell. You are building a customer-service agent, a research assistant, a scheduling agent. Your engineering team may or may not use AI to build it; that is irrelevant to the lifecycle in question. The defining problem is that your shipped artefact is stochastic. A user asks the same question twice and gets two answers. The distribution of answers shifts when you swap the model, when the retrieval corpus changes, when a tool goes down, when the season changes and users start asking about something your evaluation set never contained. The controls that follow from this are runtime controls, and the literature on them is mature enough to be conventional: Concern | Control | Output quality varies | Evaluation harnesses, golden datasets, LLM-as-judge scoring | Quality degrades silently over time | Drift monitoring, canary prompts, production sampling | Costs are unpredictable per interaction | Token economics, per-conversation budgets, model routing | Users can manipulate the agent | Prompt-injection threat modelling, red-teaming, refusal testing | Behaviour must be specified without code | Personas, standard operating procedures in natural language | Tools are the agent's hands | Tool registries, permission scoping, MCP integration | Salesforce's five phases — ideation and design, development, testing and validation, deployment and release, monitoring and tuning — map recognisably onto SDLC with the emphasis relocated toward the last phase

c: Chapter 1 — Two Meanings of ADLC, and Why the Confusion Costs You
t: 1.3 Meaning B — the agent is the labour
x: In Meaning B, the agent is your workforce. You are building a payments service, or maintaining a fifteen-year-old billing system, or migrating four hundred call sites off a deprecated API. The agent is how the work gets done. The defining problem is that your construction process is stochastic while your product remains as deterministic as it ever was. The payment service does not behave differently for each user. It behaves the way the merged code says it behaves. What varies is what the merged code says, because it was produced by a generator whose output you cannot predict. Cycode's inventory of what this breaks is the sharpest short statement available, and it is worth quoting because each item names a load-bearing assumption D: The author is a model. Attribution, accountability, and the social pressure that made code review work all assumed a human on the other side. Changes move at machine speed. Volume and velocity of code changes exceed human review capacity. The IDE is no longer the first feedback point. Code can be written, tested, and committed without a human ever seeing an editor. The pull request is no longer a natural checkpoint. It was a checkpoint because producing one was expensive. Dependencies are chosen by something that never read the package name, and has, in Cycode's phrasing, "zero understanding of organizational risk tolerance, compliance requirements, or business context." The controls that follow are not runtime monitors. They are construction-time

t: 1.4 Where the non-determinism comes to rest
x: Here is the distinction that matters, and as far as I can find it has not been stated cleanly anywhere. Everything else in this chapter is downstream of it. Ask where the randomness ends up. This single structural difference generates every downstream divergence between the two disciplines. | Meaning A — Agent-SDLC | Meaning B — ADLC | Stochastic artefact | The product | The process | Who absorbs the variance | The user, at runtime | The engineering organisation, before merge | When control ends | Never — monitoring is perpetual | At merge — the gate can be binary | Nature of controls | Probabilistic monitors, sampled | Deterministic gates plus probabilistic reviewers | Failure signature | Drift, degradation, jailbreak | Plausible-but-wrong code at machine speed | Primary metric | Output quality against an eval set | Verification capacity against generation volume | Governing question | Is the agent behaving? | Would anything have caught it if it hadn't? | Learning loop returns to | The prompt, the eval set, the model | The harness | The row that repays the most study is the third. In Meaning A there is no last interaction, so no control can ever be final; you are running a perpetual observation programme against a system that will outlive your attention. In Meaning B there is a last moment — the merge — and this is a gift. A merge gate can be deterministic. It can block. It can be a type checker, a test suite, an architecture fitness function that either passes or does not.

x: Abstract category errors are easy to shrug at. Here is the concrete damage, in both directions. Transplanting A into B. A platform team reads that the discipline requires evaluation harnesses, drift monitoring, and token economics. They build an eval set for their coding agent, dashboards for output quality, and a per-developer token budget. Twelve months later they are still measured on the same delivery metrics as before, and the reason is that they instrumented the generator instead of the constraint. Nobody measured review load per engineer per week. Nobody tracked whether static-analysis warnings were climbing. The organisation has a beautiful view of its agent's behaviour and no view at all of its own verification capacity — which is, per this book's spine, the actual bottleneck. Their apparatus was built for a problem they do not have. Transplanting B into A. A team building a customer-facing agent adopts context files, small batches, harness templates, and pre-commit sensors. Their development process is genuinely excellent — Chapter 15 would rate them at maturity Level 3. They ship. The agent is jailbroken in week two, because construction-time controls are silent about runtime adversaries, and no gate at merge time can constrain what a user will type in six months. They built a Meaning B harness around a Meaning A product. The subtler cost: agent washing, internal edition. x: The two meanings are not siblings. One contains the other, and noticing this converts a naming problem into a structural insight. Building an agent is a kind of software development. So if ADLC is the discipline of building software with agents, then building an agent with agents is simply ADLC applied to a particular product category. Meaning A is a special case of Meaning B — specifically, the case where the software under construction happens itself to be stochastic, which adds runtime obligations without removing any construction-time ones. This is not a rhetorical move. It is observable in the artefacts. Salesforce AI Research publishes a repository named agentforce-adlc, described as "Agent Development Life Cycle — Build, deploy, test, and optimize Agentforce agents using Claude Code skills and Agent Script DSL" D. Read that description slowly. It is a Meaning A framework — the agent development lifecycle, for building Agentforce agents — implemented as Claude Code skills, which is to say implemented as a Meaning B harness. Skills are one of the eight repository-level configuration mechanisms catalogued in Chapter 7. Salesforce is doing Meaning B in order to do Meaning A, and the same four letters name both layers of the sandwich. Two consequences, and the second is the useful one. x: Delegated execution under human supervision. Four words, chosen for what each excludes. Delegated — not assisted. Assistance implies the human is still performing the task with help. Delegation means the task has been handed over, and the handover is the object of study: what was specified, what authority was granted, what came back, and how it was checked. Chapter 13 turns "how much" into a five-level ladder. Execution — not generation. The unit of delegation is a task with a completion condition, not a block of text. This is the shift SWE-agent demonstrated and Chapter 2 documents: the interesting capability was never producing plausible code, it was operating in an environment until a test passed. Under human supervision — not autonomy. Supervision is a real, costed, finite resource. Treating it as free is the mechanism behind the Review Collapse anti-pattern of Chapter 21, and treating it as unnecessary is the mechanism behind most of the incidents in Chapter 11. The purpose of a harness is not to remove human input. It is to concentrate human input where judgment is irreplaceable, by mechanising everything that is not judgment.

c: Chapter 1 — Two Meanings of ADLC, and Why the Confusion Costs You
x: Three things, and they are the reason to spend a chapter on vocabulary. A defensible scope. This book is about Meaning B. Where Meaning A is relevant, it is named, bounded, and imported from deliberately. A reader can now tell whether any given piece of advice — mine or anyone else's — applies to them, by asking a single question: does the randomness ship, or does it stop at merge? A correct place to point the instruments. If the randomness stops at merge, then the merge gate is where the engineering goes, and the thing to measure is not the generator's output quality but the organisation's capacity to verify. That reorientation is what Chapters 14 and 16 are about, and it is unavailable to anyone who has not first drawn this boundary. An honest inheritance. Meaning A has solved problems Meaning B has not. Naming the boundary makes the import legitimate rather than accidental — and the most important import, the practice of specifying acceptance before implementation, is precisely the practice that Part IV argues is the last thing a human cannot delegate.

Chapter 2 — The Scaffolding Insight RAG with GPT-4 Turbo: 1.31% resolved. SWE-agent with GPT-4 Turbo: 12.47% resolved. — Table 1, Yang et al., SWE-agent, NeurIPS 2024 A Same benchmark. Same model. Same weights. Nine and a half times the result. What you'll learn: The controlled comparison that founded harness engineering, with the model held constant Why every dial on that interface turned out to be non-monotonic — including one where a tool performed worse than no tool at all Why failure was not resource-limited, and what that rules out The counter-evidence: two systems that beat elaborate scaffolding by being simpler and an order of magnitude cheaper Why the founding argument survives the discovery that a third of the benchmark was compromised The claim this chapter defends: the interface between a model and its environment is an engineering lever with a very large coefficient — but its value is non-monotonic in its richness, which makes harness engineering a design discipline with an optimum, not an accumulation exercise.

In 2023, SWE-bench asked a question that sounded modest and turned out not to be: can a language model resolve a real GitHub issue? Not write a function from a docstring — resolve an issue, in one of twelve real repositories, such that the maintainers' own unit tests pass. The first answers were humbling. Claude 2 resolved 1.96% of the benchmark A. The framing at the time was that models were not yet good enough, and the implied remedy was to wait for better models. In May 2024, a group at Princeton published a different remedy. They did not train a model. They built an interface. Their reasoning began from an analogy that has aged well. Humans do not interact with computers through raw system calls; we use editors, file browsers, and search tools, and the design of those tools measurably determines what we can accomplish. Human–computer interaction is a discipline precisely because interface design has large effects on capable operators. Language models are also operators — differently capable, differently limited — and nobody had asked what interface they need. They called it an Agent–Computer Interface, and they measured it. Read the left column first. Retrieval-augmented generation — fetch the likely-relevant files with BM25, hand them to the model, ask for a patch — resolves 1.31% with GPT-4 Turbo. The same model, given a purpose-built environment to work in, resolves 12.47%. On the Lite split the progression is visible in three stages: 2.67% with retrieval, 11.00% with

The Princeton group did something more useful than reporting a headline. They ablated their own interface — varied one dial at a time and measured what happened. This is Table 3 of the paper, and it is, I think, the most under-read table in the literature. Look at what these four rows have in common. The file viewer. Showing the agent 100 lines at a time scores 18.0%. Showing it 30 lines scores 14.3% — too little to reason with. Showing it the entire file scores 12.7%, which is worse than either. More information, less capability. The curve has a peak and the generous side falls further than the stingy side. Context retention. Keeping the last five observations scores 18.0%. Keeping the full history scores 15.0%. The agent given complete memory of its own session performs worse than the agent given a sliding window. The editor. No edit command at all: 10.3%, and the paper explains why — without a purpose-built editor the agent falls back to sed and shell redirection, both of which are error-prone for multi-line changes and, crucially, provide "lack immediate feedback about file updates, making these silent operations potentially confusing for models to interpret." Adding an edit command: 15.0%. Adding a linter that rejects the edit if it would introduce a syntax error: 18.0%. That last increment is worth pausing on, because it is the first sensor in this book. t: 2.3 The tool that was worse than no tool
x: Now the search row, which is the most instructive line in the table and the reason this chapter exists. No search capability at all: 15.7% Iterative search — results shown one at a time, next and prev to page through, each match displayed with surrounding context: 12.0% Summarised search — all matches listed at once, with guidance to refine the query if there are too many: 18.0% Iterative search is a good interface. It is what Vim does. It is what VS Code does. It is the design that decades of human interface work converged on, because a human paging through matches builds a mental model as they go and stops when they have found what they need. Agents did not stop. From the paper: "when given a large number of search results, agents tend to look through every match exhaustively, calling next until each result has been inspected. This inefficient behavior can exhaust an agent's cost budget or context window." The intervention made things worse than the absence of the intervention — 12.0% against 15.7%, a deficit of nearly four points against doing nothing at all. Taleb calls this iatrogenics: harm caused by the healer. His examples are medical — the treatment whose side effects exceed the disease — and his argument is that iatrogenics is systematically under-counted, because the harm from action is attributed to the illness while the harm from inaction is attributed to the physician. Engineering has the same asymmetry. Nobody is blamed for the linter they did not write. Everyb

One more finding from the same paper, because it forecloses the most common intervention. The authors observed that "agents succeed quickly and fail slowly." Successful instances finished with a median cost of \$1.21 across 12 steps. Unsuccessful ones consumed a mean of \$2.52 across 21 steps. And the decisive number: 93.0% of resolved instances were submitted before exhausting the cost budget, against 69.0% of instances overall. Their conclusion is stated without hedging: "increasing the maximum budget or token limit are unlikely to substantially increase performance." The failures were not agents that ran out of room. They were agents that had gone wrong early and were spending the remainder of their budget going wronger. The paper's failure taxonomy confirms it — roughly 52% of unresolved instances were classified as incorrect or overly specific implementations, and a further 23.4% as cascading failed edits. Very few were "ran out of time." This matters because "give it a bigger budget" is the first thing every organisation tries, and it is the intervention most likely to be measured as a cost increase with no corresponding benefit. If most failures are wrong-direction failures rather than insufficient-resource failures, then the corrective is a sensor that detects the wrong direction early, not a larger allowance to continue in it. This is the argument for keeping quality left that Chapter 8 develops, and here it has an empirical basis rather than a rhetorical one. There

If the chapter stopped here it would be propaganda. The naive inference from §2.1 — interfaces matter, therefore build elaborate interfaces — is false, and two systems demonstrate it. Agentless, published two months after SWE-agent, asked whether the agent loop was necessary at all. It replaced autonomous exploration with a fixed three-phase pipeline: localise, repair, validate. No planning, no tool selection, no trajectory. On SWE-bench Lite it achieved 27.33% at an average cost of \$0.34 — at the time the highest performance and the lowest cost of any open-source approach, later improved to 32.00% B. Set the two side by side, and compute what the papers do not: | Resolve rate (Lite) | Cost per attempt | Cost per resolved issue | RAG, GPT-4 Turbo | 2.67% | \$0.13 | \$4.87 | SWE-agent, GPT-4 Turbo | 18.00% | \$1.67 | \$9.28 | Agentless | 27.33% | \$0.34 | \$1.24 | (Third column derived: average cost ÷ resolve rate. Arithmetic is mine, inputs are the published figures.) The elaborate interface bought reach — it resolved issues that retrieval could not touch — but it did so at roughly twice the cost per resolved issue. And a well-designed pipeline with no agent loop at all beat it on both axes at once, resolving half again as many issues for a seventh of the cost each. mini-swe-agent completes the arc. It is one hundred lines of Python. It has no tools other than bash — it does not even use the models' tool-calling interface. It has no configuration surface to speak of. It scor

t: 2.6 Reconciliation: the harness compensates for deficits
x: These findings are not in conflict once you ask what the interface was for. The 2024 ACI was not adding capability. It was compensating for specific model deficits, and the ablation table names each one: Interface element | The deficit it compensated for | Edit command | Poor multi-line editing through shell primitives | Linting guardrail | Inability to recover from self-inflicted syntax errors | 100-line viewer | Degraded reasoning over very long file contents | Last-5-observations window | Degraded reasoning over long histories | Summarised search | No satiety signal — would exhaust an enumerable list | Every one of those is a statement about a 2024-era model. And every one of them is the kind of deficit that subsequent training closes. When the deficit closes, the compensation does not become neutral — it becomes overhead. The scaffold that was carrying the model is now constraining it, occupying context that the model no longer needs spent on its behalf. This produces the most actionable prescription in the chapter, and it runs against every instinct an engineering organisation has: A mature harness gets smaller when the model improves. Taleb's via negativa — the observation that in complex systems, removal is more reliable than addition, because you can be confident about what harm you have eliminated and only hopeful about what benefit you have introduced — is not a metaphor here. It is the operating procedure. Chapter 8 turns it into a practice: every element of a harn

Everything above rests on SWE-bench. So it is necessary to say plainly what SWE-bench is, and it is not what most people who cite it believe. Taleb's ludic fallacy is the error of mistaking the tidy, bounded uncertainty of a game for the messy, unbounded uncertainty of the world. In a casino the probabilities are known, the rules are fixed, and the game ends. Outside, none of that holds — yet people trained on games reason about the world as though it were one. SWE-bench is a casino, in three specific ways. It supplies ground truth that real work does not have. Every instance comes with the maintainers' own tests: a set that must go from failing to passing, and a set that must stay passing. That is a complete, machine-checkable specification of success, delivered free, before the work begins. Chapter 8's behaviour-harness problem exists precisely because real tasks arrive without this. The benchmark hands out, at the start of every instance, the artefact whose absence is the field's central unsolved problem. A third of it leaked. The SWE-Bench+ study found that 32.67% of successful patches involved solution leakage — the fix was present in the issue report or its comments — and that a further 31.08% of passing patches were suspicious due to weak tests that could not distinguish a correct patch from a plausible one B. A separate study using differential patch testing found 7.8% of patches counted as correct while failing the developers' own test suite B. And when it was cleane

Having said that, the argument of this chapter is unharmed, and the reason is worth more than the argument itself, because it generalises to every contaminated measurement you will ever be handed. Contamination destroys absolute claims. It leaves relative claims standing, provided it is symmetric across the arms. Solution leakage does not know which interface is reading the issue. If a fix is written in the issue comments, it is equally available to the RAG baseline, the shell-only agent, and SWE-agent. Weak tests are equally weak for all three. The contamination is a property of the instances, and every arm of the comparison ran on the same instances. So the correct reading is not "SWE-agent resolves 12.47% of real GitHub issues." It never was. The correct reading is: On a fixed set of tasks, holding the model constant, replacing retrieval with a purpose-built interface multiplied the resolve rate by roughly nine. On the same fixed set of tasks, four separate interface dials each showed an interior optimum, and one tool performed worse than its own absence. Every clause survives cleaning, because cleaning removes instances from both arms. This is a habit worth acquiring, because you will need it constantly. Almost every number quoted at you about agent performance is a level. Levels are the fragile kind. When you are told a tool "resolves 70% of issues," the question is not whether the number is honest — it probably is — but what it is a level of, and whether anything held c

Four claims are now on solid ground, and one that is often bundled with them is not. Licensed. Interface design has a large causal effect on agent capability, independent of the model. Controlled comparison, model held constant, ratio robust to contamination. Licensed. That effect is non-monotonic in richness. Four dials, four interior optima, one control worse than its own absence. Licensed. Most failures are misdirection, not scarcity. Successful runs are cheaper and shorter; 93% of successes finish inside budget. Licensed. The optimal harness shrinks as the model improves. Three systems across two years, each simpler and cheaper than the last, each scoring higher. Not licensed — and this is the inference the field makes constantly — that a higher benchmark score means a tool will work better on your codebase. SWE-bench instances come with ground-truth tests, are drawn from twelve public Python repositories, and are shaped like bug fixes. If your work involves a private codebase, an unstated specification, or a change that is not a bug fix, the benchmark is measuring a different game. Chapter 21 names the error Benchmark Cargo Cult and it is the ludic fallacy wearing a procurement badge. The honest summary of what Princeton demonstrated is smaller than the headline and more useful: The environment an agent works in is a designed artefact with measurable effects, an interior optimum, and no guarantee that adding to it helps. That sentence is the licence for everything in Par

The interface is a lever with a very large coefficient and an interior optimum, which means a harness must be measured rather than accumulated — and must shrink as the model it compensates for improves.

What is the current optimum? Every number in Figure 2.2 was measured against 2024 models. The dials almost certainly have different peaks now, and nobody has re-run the ablation. This is a cheap, high-value replication that the field has not done. Is there a general theory of harness–model fit? The Claude/GPT-4 inversion in Figure 2.1 shows that the optimal interface differs by model. If so, harnesses are not portable across model swaps, which has uncomfortable implications for the harness templates of Chapter 8. Does the compensation curve hold at organisational scale? Figure 2.3 is a conjecture drawn through three data points from public benchmarks. Whether an enterprise harness also shrinks with model capability — or whether organisational controls, unlike model compensations, only ratchet upward — is unmeasured and matters more than the benchmark question.

Chapter 3 — The Productivity Paradox "An enterprise AI mandate is a process-redesign problem, not a tooling deployment: the gain grows with use rather than arriving overnight, and it relocates work downstream rather than removing it." — He, Agarwal, Denisov-Blanch, Azaletskiy, Koyejo, Vasilescu, arXiv 2607.01904 B What you'll learn: The five best-measured points on the productivity question, and why they form a gradient rather than a contradiction Three instruments — stated, measured, and revealed preference — that give three different answers about the same tools Why individual gains do not automatically become organisational gains, derived from queueing rather than asserted The four ways a saturated review system can respond, and which one a real enterprise actually chose Why "merge and revert rates held steady" is a statement about a measurement window, not a reassurance The claim this chapter defends: individual velocity gains are real, large, and can even survive aggregation — but the work is relocated onto review rather than removed, and every available response to that relocation either lengthens delivery, degrades scrutiny, enlarges batches, or replaces human review with machine review. Choosing deliberately among those four is what a lifecycle is for.

The literature on AI and developer productivity looks like a shouting match. It is not. It is a well-behaved gradient that nobody plots, because plotting it requires citing studies that disagree with you. Here are the five best-measured points, all verified against primaries. +55.8%. Peng, Kalliamvakou, Cihon, and Demirer recruited developers and asked them to implement an HTTP server in JavaScript as quickly as possible. The group with Copilot finished 55.8% faster A. This is the number in every vendor deck. The task is greenfield, self-contained, specified in a sentence, and touches no existing code. +26.08%. Cui, Demirer, Jaffe, Musolff, Peng, and Salz pooled three randomised controlled trials run at Microsoft, Accenture, and an anonymous Fortune 100 company as part of ordinary business. Across 4,867 developers, completed tasks rose 26.08% — with a standard error of 10.3%, which is a confidence interval wide enough to deserve mention every time the point estimate is quoted. Published in Management Science A. Less experienced developers adopted more and gained more. +21%. A Google enterprise trial put 96 engineers on a realistic internal task — a logging service, ten files, 474 lines of code — with and without three AI features. The AI group finished in 96 minutes against 114: 21% faster. And then the honest part, which is why this study deserves more citation than it gets: when the authors controlled for developer-level and task-level factors, the effect held at roughly 21

Before the mechanism, the epistemics, because a reader who has not resolved this will not accept the mechanism. We have three ways to ask whether these tools help, and they disagree systematically. Instrument | Method | Answer | Stated preference | Ask developers | METR cohort forecast +24% beforehand; estimated +20% afterwards | Measured outcome | Time the tasks | −19% | Revealed preference | Offer money to abstain | 30–50% refused to submit tasks they were unwilling to do without AI, at \$50/hour | The third row is the one almost nobody cites, and it is the most interesting. When METR ran a follow-up, so many developers declined to work without AI that the selection effect forced a redesign of the experiment B. These are not survey responses. They are choices with a price attached, and the price was declined. The temptation is to pick a winner. Resist it, because each instrument is valid for something different and the disagreement is informative. Stated preference measures experience, and it is wrong about duration. The METR result is not that developers lie. It is that they were 19% slower and could not feel it, after living through it. Something about the experience of delegating — less waiting on your own recall, less friction, more of the session spent reading fluent output — registers as speed regardless of the clock. Taleb's general warning about introspection applies with unusual force: the feeling of a process is not evidence about the process. Chapter 18 takes thi

In June 2025 the CTO of a mid-sized commercial B2B software company sent an email to an R&D organisation of several hundred engineers. The goal: double engineering productivity through AI adoption over twelve months. The designated progress metric: merged pull requests per engineer per month. Researchers from Carnegie Mellon and Stanford were given access to the telemetry. The resulting study covers 802 developers and 196,212 non-bot pull requests across 364 repositories, from January 2024 to April 2026 B. The authors describe the site as near-ideal and unusually favourable: young, AI-forward, permissive, provisioning commercial tools with no per-seat caps or token budgets. If large gains exist anywhere, they should appear here. They did. Mean pull requests per active developer rose from 21.2 in the pre-mandate baseline to 44.3 in April 2026 — a 2.09× increase. Company-wide pull request volume grew 3.1×. Token spend among pull-request authors rose roughly 20×. The share of AI-authored pull requests climbed from near zero to about 90%. Among the 246 developers present throughout, mean throughput rose 2.3×. Controlling for calendar time, the within-developer gain was +0.54 log points (1.72×), and +0.38 (1.46×) under full calendar-month fixed effects — conservative, and still large. The mandate was met. Per-capita merged pull requests roughly doubled in twelve months. This is an inconvenient result for the pessimistic reading of §3.1, and it should be stated without softening: a

t: 3.4 The team boundary is a queue
x: Why should doubling generation double reviewer load rather than doubling delivery? Because the pipeline is not a sequence of independent stages. It contains a shared server with finite capacity, and that changes the arithmetic entirely. Start with the weaker bound, which is already sobering. Amdahl's law: if authoring code is a fraction f of total cycle time and you speed that fraction by factor S, overall improvement is 1 / ((1−f) + f/S). Suppose authoring is 30% of cycle time. Doubling authoring speed yields 17.6%. Making authoring instantaneous — infinite speedup — yields 43%, and not one point more. Under this model there is a ceiling and it is low. But review is not merely another stage. It is a queue with servers, and queues do not degrade linearly. For a single-server queue, time in system is W = 1/(μ−λ). As arrivals approach capacity, ρ → 1 and W diverges. This is not a metaphor; it is why motorway traffic collapses at a specific density and why an on-call rotation at 90% utilisation feels categorically worse than one at 70%. The enterprise study reports per-reviewer load roughly doubling — λ per server doubled — while a large-scale telemetry study across 10,000+ developers and 1,255 teams reports the accompanying symptoms: +98% merged pull requests, +91% review time, +154% average PR size, +9% bugs, and no measurable improvement in organisational DORA metrics D — vendor data, so graded accordingly, but the shape is exactly what Figure 3.3 predicts and it corroborates

t: 3.5 Four valves, all of them costly
x: When ρ approaches 1, a real organisation does not diverge to infinity. It does one or more of four things. There is no fifth. Now read the evidence back against the diagram, and notice that the two organisations we have real data for pulled valves 3 and 4. Valve 3 was pulled, measurably. Average PR size rose 37% on adoption and a further 33% post-mandate in the enterprise study; the telemetry study reports +154%. Larger batches reduce the item count arriving at review, which relieves λ. They also make each item harder to review well, and DORA identifies working in small batches as one of the seven capabilities that determine whether AI benefits reach the organisation at all C. So the organisation relieved queue pressure by moving away from the practice most associated with the outcome it wanted. Nobody decided this. It is what a system under pressure does. Valve 4 was pulled, decisively. Automated review overtook human review. Bots reached ~38% of review events and ~half of all review comments. Here is what I find genuinely remarkable about that finding, and it is the bridge to the rest of the book. Nobody in this book's framework told that company to build inferential sensors. They were not following a lifecycle. They had a throughput mandate and a review queue that was saturating, and under that pressure they independently invented the thing Chapter 7 calls an inferential feedback control — a model-based reviewer inserted into the loop because the human one could not scale.

The enterprise study reports that merge and revert rates did not move. AI-authored code, reviewed increasingly by machines, shipped without a measurable quality penalty. Take that seriously. It is real evidence against the alarmist reading, and this book's second commitment requires stating it in its strongest form: on the quality proxies available, at the scale of a year, substituting automated review for human review did not visibly hurt. Then read what the authors themselves say those proxies are: "AI-generated code now ships under automated review without a measurable penalty on these coarse, short-horizon quality proxies." Coarse. Short-horizon. Their words, and they matter enormously, because we can situate them against a study by the same lead author. Hao He is first author both here and on the difference-in-differences study of Cursor adoption across public repositories, whose title states its finding: Speed at the Cost of Quality? How Cursor AI Increases Short-Term Velocity and Long-Term Complexity in Software Projects A. Velocity gains: large, transient. Complexity and static-analysis warnings: substantial, persistent. So one researcher, two datasets, two horizons, two findings that only appear to conflict: A revert happens within days. Complexity accretion is visible over months. Duplication over quarters. The proxies that stayed flat are precisely the ones whose window closes before the documented damage becomes visible. Taleb calls the general error the turkey pr

Return to the CTO's email. The mandate was to double engineering productivity. The designated metric was merged pull requests per engineer per month. That metric went from 21.2 to 44.3. But average PR size rose roughly 37% on adoption and a further 33% after the mandate. So a pull request in April 2026 was not the same object as a pull request in April 2025. The unit drifted. This does not mean the gain was illusory — more, larger pull requests is unambiguously more code shipped, and the token spend and volume figures confirm real work happened. It means something more specific and more troubling: the organisation hit its target while the unit of review got larger, which is to say while reviewability degraded. This is Goodhart's law operating exactly as advertised — when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — with the twist that the corruption was not gaming. Nobody split or padded pull requests to make a number. The metric was hit honestly, and hitting it honestly required the batch growth that made the underlying goal harder to achieve. The enterprise study cites Miller and colleagues on a related failure they name the productivity pressure paradox: a mandate that raises expectations without granting time to build skill undermines the gains it seeks B. And Storey's reframing is the sharpest available description of what accumulates: not technical debt exactly, but cognitive and intent debt — the gap that opens when code outpaces a team's capacity to ab

Everything in this chapter reduces to five statements. Each is supported above; none requires the others to be believed on faith. 1. Individual gains are real and large. +55.8% on scoped tasks, +26.08% across 4,867 developers in three RCTs, +40% in heaviest-usage weeks across 16,223 engineers. 2. They shrink to zero, and can invert, as the work becomes expert work in familiar code. −19%, in the most controlled study of that setting we have. 3. They can nonetheless aggregate. 2.09× per-capita merged pull requests over twelve months in a favourable enterprise setting; 3.1× company-wide volume. 4. But the work is relocated, not removed, and it lands on review. Per-reviewer load roughly doubled in the same study. 5. Every response to that relocation costs something. Lead time, scrutiny, reviewability, or the engineering effort to mechanise review. The organisation studied paid in reviewability (+37% batch size) and mechanisation (automated review overtaking human review), and its short-horizon quality proxies stayed flat over a window too short to detect the effects the long-horizon studies report. Which yields the sentence this book exists for: Verification capacity is the constraint. Generation capacity is not. An organisation that increases the second without increasing the first has not become faster; it has moved its bottleneck somewhere less visible. The remaining twenty-four chapters are about increasing μ deliberately. Part II builds the apparatus. Part III makes it a lif

Individual gains are real and can aggregate, but they relocate work onto review rather than removing it — and since review capacity cannot be bought with tokens or reliably with headcount, mechanising part of verification is the only lever that raises the constraint rather than moving it out of sight.

Where is ρ for a given team, and can it be measured directly? The queueing account in §3.4 is a model fitted to reported symptoms, not an estimate from instrumented queues. Nobody has published review utilisation as a first-class metric, which Chapter 14 argues is the single most valuable missing measurement in the field. Does valve 4 hold? Automated review absorbed the load with flat short-horizon quality proxies. Whether that survives a five-year window is unmeasured, and it is the most consequential unanswered question in this chapter. If it does not hold, the enterprise in §3.3 has bought throughput on credit. How much of the enterprise gain was model improvement rather than accumulated skill? The study's own authors flag that the gain is "not separable across model generations," with three frontier releases inside their window. The dose–response and the release ladder are confounded, and they say so. Is the gradient in Figure 3.1 a gradient of task realism or of specification completeness? Every high-scoring study supplied a clear specification; METR's real tasks did not. If it is the latter, the remedy is specification discipline rather than harness scope, and Chapter 22 has to take that possibility seriously.

Chapter 4 — The Debt Ledger "A statistically significant, large, but transient increase in project-level development velocity… a substantial and persistent increase in static analysis warnings and code complexity… major factors driving long-term velocity slowdown." — He, Miller, Agarwal, Kästner, Vasilescu, MSR '26, arXiv 2511.04427 A What you'll learn: Why debt is the hardest claim in this field to establish, and why that difficulty is itself the finding The four signals that are actually measured, and the one study with a causal design The counter-evidence, presented in full, including the study that found no penalty at all Why generated code would accumulate structural debt even if every individual change were correct The negative feedback loop that maintained codebases for fifty years, why delegation removes it, and what has to be installed in its place The claim this chapter defends: the ledger is asymmetric in measurability before it is asymmetric in outcome — velocity is prompt, countable, and attributable while structural cost is deferred, contestable, and ownerless. Combined with the removal of the only negative feedback loop that ever regulated code structure, this makes accumulation the default rather than an accident, and it makes a lifecycle rather than a tool the necessary response.

t: 4.1 The hardest chapter to write honestly
x: Chapter 3 ended with an organisation whose merge and revert rates did not budge across twelve months of near-total AI adoption. If quality had collapsed, that is where it would have shown. So this chapter has an obligation. The literature on AI and code quality is the part of this field most contaminated by motivated reasoning, and a book that has spent three chapters demanding verified figures cannot now reach for the alarming ones. Begin with the reason the question is hard, because it is not a shortage of data. Debt is a counterfactual. To claim that a codebase has accumulated debt is to claim that a different codebase — the one that would have existed under different practice — would have been cheaper to change. That codebase does not exist. It cannot be inspected. Every debt measurement is therefore a proxy standing in for an unobservable comparison, and the proxies are all contestable. Consider what "high complexity" actually asserts. Cyclomatic complexity counts branches. A function with many branches may be badly factored, or it may be correctly handling a domain with many cases. A static-analysis warning may flag a real defect or a false positive that the team has correctly learned to ignore. Duplication may be copy-paste debt or it may be two things that resemble each other today and will diverge tomorrow, which is exactly when premature extraction becomes the more expensive mistake. None of these proxies is worthless. All of them are arguable. And this is the struc

Four signals, in descending order of evidential strength. Complexity and static-analysis warnings. The strongest design in the field, and the epigraph of this chapter. He, Miller, Agarwal, Kästner, and Vasilescu ran a difference-in-differences analysis comparing GitHub projects that adopted Cursor against a matched control group of similar non-adopting projects, published at MSR '26 A. Difference-in-differences with matched controls is the right tool for exactly this question: it estimates what happened to adopters relative to what would plausibly have happened otherwise. It is the closest anyone has come to constructing the missing counterfactual. Their finding has three parts, and the third is the one usually dropped: 1. Velocity increased — "statistically significant, large, but transient." 2. Static-analysis warnings and code complexity increased — "substantial and persistent." 3. Those increases were "major factors driving long-term velocity slowdown." The third clause converts a correlation into a mechanism. It is not merely that debt accumulated alongside a fading speed-up. The accumulated debt is identified as a driver of the fade. A caveat I am obliged to state: the specific percentages circulating in secondary coverage of this paper — figures around +28% lines added, +30% warnings, +41% complexity, and a repository count of 806 — are not verified here. I retrieved the abstract and the venue; the effect sizes live in the full paper. This book does not print unverifie

Now the other side, and it deserves the same care. Short-horizon quality proxies did not move in the best-documented enterprise case. In the twelve-month "2×" mandate study of 802 developers, merge rate and revert rate held steady while AI-authored pull requests rose to about 90% of the total and automated review overtook human review B. On the measures available, code shipped under machine review without visible penalty. A controlled experiment found no maintainability penalty. The same enterprise study cites a controlled experiment finding no maintainability penalty when later developers evolve AI-co-developed code — and, in fact, confirming a speed-up when they did so 🔴 (cited within, primary not retrieved). If that result holds and generalises, it attacks the debt thesis at its foundation, because the entire concern is precisely that future changes become more expensive. The strongest debt evidence is observational. He et al.'s difference-in-differences is a good design, but it is applied to public repositories with self-selected tool adoption. Projects that adopt Cursor may differ from matched controls in ways matching does not capture — appetite for velocity, team composition, growth stage. The authors are careful; the design is still not a randomised trial. GitClear is a vendor. Its business is code-change analytics. This does not make its figures wrong — the moved-code trend in particular is a mechanical measurement that would be difficult to fake and easy to falsify

Most of that apparent conflict dissolves the way Chapter 3's did. Reverts detect acute failure — something broke and someone noticed within days. Complexity accretion is chronic. A codebase does not revert because a function acquired three extra branches; it becomes, six quarters later, a codebase where every change takes longer, and by then no individual change is blameable. This gives the honest formulation of what we know: On acute, short-horizon quality proxies, agent-authored code under automated review shows no measured penalty. On chronic, structural proxies over multi-year windows, the one quasi-experimental study available finds substantial and persistent degradation that it identifies as driving later slowdown. Nobody has measured both, on the same codebase, over a window long enough to settle it. That is a less satisfying sentence than "AI is destroying your codebase." It is also the true one, and Chapter 27 lists the longitudinal study that would resolve it as an open problem.

Here is where the chapter stops reporting and starts arguing, and the argument does not depend on any of the contested figures. Ask why generated code would accumulate structural debt even if every individual change were correct. Not incorrect. Correct. Every diff passes review, every test goes green, every requirement is satisfied. Does structure still degrade? I think it does, necessarily, and the reason is a cost gradient. Consider a routine situation: a change needs behaviour that already exists somewhere, slightly differently. There are two correct implementations. Option A — duplicate and modify. Copy the existing logic, adjust it, use it locally. Correct. Touches one file. Breaks nothing. Option B — extract and reuse. Pull the shared behaviour into a common abstraction, adapt both call sites. Also correct. Touches several files. Risks every existing caller. Now price both options for each kind of author. Three things are doing work here. The agent's cost of Option B is genuinely higher than a human's, for structural reasons. Extraction requires knowing every call site. That is a repository-wide question answered from partial observation — precisely the hardest thing for an operator working through a bounded context window. Chapter 9's entire argument for graph engineering is that this question is currently answered badly. The agent's cost of Option A is genuinely lower. No cross-file reasoning, no risk to existing callers, no need to hold the whole dependency structure

There is a deeper version of this, and it is the chapter's real contribution. Complexity, under purely additive change, is monotone. Add a branch, complexity rises. Add a special case, complexity rises. Nothing in the ordinary business of satisfying requirements ever removes a branch. If a system only ever receives additive change, its complexity grows without bound, and this is true of human-written code as well. Human codebases did not grow without bound. Why not? Because they contained a negative feedback loop that nobody designed and nobody measured. Periodically, a maintainer's discomfort exceeded their tolerance and they cleaned something up. Not because a ticket demanded it. Because it had become unpleasant. That is a homeostat: a mechanism that senses a deviation and acts to reduce it, keeping a variable within bounds without any external controller. This reframing matters because it changes what the remedy is. If you believe agents produce debt, the remedy is to make them produce less of it — better prompts, stricter rules, more review. If you believe delegation removed a homeostat, the remedy is to install a replacement, and the replacement must have the properties the original had: it must sense the deviation without being asked, and it must act without waiting for a ticket.
