Chapter 5 — What Actually Breaks "It is not enough to know that a fence stands in a field. Before you remove it, you must know what it was keeping out." — after G. K. Chesterton What you'll learn: The five assumptions SDLC never wrote down, because nobody had to pay for them Why a pull request was a checkpoint by cost rather than by design, and what that means now Why the failures are simultaneous rather than sequential — the single common cause A diagnostic you can run this week: which of your gates are cost-derived and therefore debased Why this is not Agile or DevOps done properly, and the honest answer to "degree or kind?" The claim this chapter defends: software engineering's process gates were largely purchased by the expense of writing code, not designed. Scrutiny, intent, pacing, a trust boundary, and structural self-correction all arrived free as side effects of that expense. Cheap generation withdraws the payment, so all five fail at once — which is why the response has to be a lifecycle that buys them explicitly, and why no tool can supply them.

Chapter 1 quoted an inventory of what breaks: the author is a model, changes move at machine speed, the IDE is no longer the first feedback point, the pull request is no longer a natural checkpoint, and dependencies are chosen by something that never read the package name D. It is a good list, and Cycode deserves credit for assembling it early. This chapter asks the two questions the list does not: why does each item fail, and what do they have in common? The answer to the second question turns out to determine the whole shape of the book, so I will state it now and spend the chapter earning it. Every one of those failures traces to the same source. Software engineering's most important controls were never designed. They were side effects of the price of code. For fifty years, writing a line of working software was expensive — in time, in attention, in the scarce supply of people who could do it — and that expense quietly purchased five distinct goods that no methodology document ever claims credit for, because nobody was billed for them. This is the reason tools cannot fix what is breaking. The five goods were not in any tool. They were in the price. It is also why the failure feels bewildering to experienced engineers. Nothing in their training identified these as mechanisms, because from the inside they did not look like mechanisms. They looked like how software works. You do not notice the ballast until the ship rides high. Taleb's recurring warning is that efficiency cam

t: 5.2 Assumption 1 — production is the expensive step
x: What was assumed. That the scarce resource is the capacity to produce correct code, and therefore that the lifecycle should be organised around producing it: specify so implementation is unambiguous, design so implementation is tractable, test what implementation produced, release it. Why it failed. Chapter 3, in one line: generation is elastic and review is not. A team can multiply its output of pull requests by adding tokens; it cannot multiply its capacity to understand them by any comparable means. The best-documented enterprise case doubled per-capita merged pull requests in twelve months and doubled per-reviewer load in the same period B. Brooks explained in 1975 why the second number cannot be fixed by hiring. What this invalidates. Not just the ordering of phases — the object of optimisation. Every methodology since the 1970s competed on how to get to working implementation faster and with fewer defects. Agile shortened the loop. DevOps automated the path to production. Both are optimisations of a pipeline whose expensive stage has moved. The replacement. Verification capacity becomes the managed constraint: measured (Chapter 14), staffed and organised for (Chapter 16), and partially mechanised (Chapters 7–8), because Chapter 3's four valves leave no other option that actually raises capacity. This is the assumption whose failure everyone already accepts in principle. The remaining four are the ones that surprise people.

t: 5.3 Assumption 2 — effort is evidence of care
x: This is the deepest failure and the least discussed, so it gets the most space. What was assumed. That the existence of a change implies someone reasoned about it. Nobody wrote this down either. But consider what a pull request meant in 2015. Someone had read enough of the codebase to find the right file. They had held the problem in their head long enough to form an approach. They had typed it, watched it fail, and fixed it. By the time the request existed, hours of human cognition had been spent, and the artefact was evidence of the cognition. That evidentiary relationship is what made code review work. A reviewer was not auditing from zero. They were checking a considered artefact produced by a colleague who had already eliminated the obvious errors. Review could be cheap precisely because authorship was expensive. Chapter 1 noted that the pull request is no longer a natural checkpoint. Here is the mechanism, and it is worth stating carefully because it generalises: The pull request was never a checkpoint by design. It was a checkpoint by cost. Its authority came entirely from the expense of producing one. Remove the expense and the gate remains in the process diagram while its informational content goes to zero. Note what Figure 5.2 does not claim. It does not say agent-authored changes are careless. Chapter 3 found flat merge and revert rates across 196,212 pull requests, and Chapter 4 conceded that a controlled experiment reportedly found no maintainability penalty. Car

t: 5.4 Assumption 3 — the author has intent you can interrogate
x: What was assumed. That behind every change stands someone who knows why, and can be asked. Code review is a social protocol before it is a technical one. Its central move is a question: why did you do it this way? The answer recovers information that is not in the diff — which alternatives were considered, which constraint forced the shape, which convention was being honoured. Ozkaya's observation is that architecture knowledge encodes why, and why is not recoverable from what D 🔴. Why it failed. The author now has no memory of the session, no stake in the outcome, no reputation among the people who will maintain the code, and no expectation of being the one called at three in the morning. Ask an agent why and you will receive a fluent, plausible reconstruction generated after the fact — which is worse than no answer, because it is indistinguishable from a real one. Chapter 4 met the same failure from the structural side. The reason human codebases resisted entropy was a felt cost — call it taste — that opposed the cheap option. That feeling was the same faculty that answered why. Both were properties of having a person there. What this invalidates. Review as dialogue. What remains is review as inspection: you can check the artefact against stated criteria, but you cannot recover unstated intent by asking. And this is where Chapter 0's closing line stops being rhetoric and becomes an engineering constraint: A harness cannot verify correctness against a requirement that was ne

t: 5.5 Assumption 4 — feedback arrives faster than change
x: What was assumed. That the loop is faster than the process it observes. This is the premise beneath continuous integration, shift-left, trunk-based development, and small batches: catch problems while they are cheap, which requires catching them soon, which requires the detector to outrun the change. Why it failed. Chapter 3's arithmetic. Arrival rate rose by a factor of two to three; review capacity did not move. When λ approaches μ, the queue's response time diverges, and the detector is no longer ahead of the process — it is behind it, working on a state of the world that has already been superseded. There is a control-systems statement of this, and it is not a metaphor: a regulator slower than its plant does not regulate it. It produces an output that was appropriate to a past state. In signal terms, sampling a process more slowly than it changes does not merely give you an incomplete picture; it gives you a wrong one, because the samples alias into a pattern that was never there. A reviewer working through a backlog of week-old pull requests against a codebase that has moved twice since is not reviewing slowly. They are reviewing something else. What this invalidates. Not the principle — keeping quality left remains correct, and Chapter 8 develops it. What is invalidated is the assumption that human review can be the left-most meaningful control. If the detector must outrun the change, and change is now machine-paced, then the left-most controls must be machine-paced too

What was assumed. That the trust boundary of a software project runs around write access. Everything inside — source, configuration, build scripts — is instruction, and is therefore controlled. Everything outside — issue text, pull-request comments, documentation, package names, error messages, web pages — is data, and is therefore safe to read. This assumption was so solid it was never a security control at all; it was the substrate the security controls were built on. Why it failed. An agent reading an issue in order to fix it cannot reliably separate the description of a problem from an instruction about what to do. OWASP's 2026 Top 10 for Agentic Applications ranks Agent Goal Hijacking (ASI01) first, on exactly this basis: because agents cannot reliably distinguish instructions from data, a single poisoned input can redirect an agent to cause harm using its own legitimate tools and access C. The structural consequence is a change in who can attack you, and it deserves stating as starkly as it deserves: Previously an attacker needed write access to a trusted repository. Now they need the ability to open an issue. What this invalidates. The location of the trust boundary, and therefore most of the reasoning built on top of it. Code review protected the inside; nothing protected the reading of the outside, because reading was never dangerous. The replacement. Every artefact an agent reads is treated as untrusted instruction; capability scoping is designed on the assumption t

t: 5.7 The sixth, and the common cause
x: Chapter 4 spent itself on a sixth assumption: that structure self-corrects. Complexity is monotone under additive change, and human codebases stayed bounded only because they contained an unmeasured negative feedback loop — a maintainer's discomfort exceeding tolerance. Delegation removed the loop and multiplied the input rate. Line the six up and the pattern in Figure 5.1 is unmistakable. # | The assumption | What was actually paying for it | 1 | Production is the expensive step | It was the expensive step | 2 | Effort is evidence of care | The price of producing an artefact | 3 | The author has interrogable intent | A person being there | 4 | Feedback outruns change | Change being slow because production was slow | 5 | Only code is instruction | Contribution requiring expensive access | 6 | Structure self-corrects | A person feeling discomfort | Six rows, and the right-hand column has two entries: the price of production and the presence of a person. And the second reduces to the first, because a person was there only because production required one. So the six failures are one failure, observed from six angles. Which explains three things that are otherwise puzzling. Why they are simultaneous. Nobody removed six controls. One thing was withdrawn, and six goods were resting on it. Why they were invisible. None was designed, so none was documented, so none appeared in any methodology's list of what it depends on. You cannot audit a dependency nobody declared. Why tools canno

t: 5.8 Why this is not Agile or DevOps done properly
x: The obvious objection, and it deserves a direct answer. Agile and DevOps were responses to real constraints and they worked. Agile attacked the problem that requirements were unknowable in advance, and its remedy was to shorten the loop between building and learning. DevOps attacked the problem that getting working code into production was slow and manual, and its remedy was to automate the path. Look at what both remedies presuppose. | Agile / DevOps assumed | ADLC must build | The unit of work | A human-authored increment | A task an agent completes; unit must be enforced, not assumed | Feedback | The loop is faster than the change | Detectors must be machine-paced to stay ahead | Review | A meaningful human gate exists | Authority reallocated from social to computational gates | Intent | Lives in the team's shared understanding | Externalised ahead of generation, machine-checkable | Inputs | Data | Potentially adversarial instruction | Structure | Craftspeople maintain it | Standing sensors with a mandate | Every remedy in the left column stands on the same withdrawn pillar. Shift-left is a strategy for a world where the detector outruns the change. Small batches is a strategy that presumes the batch size is chosen. Trunk-based development presumes each commit was considered. These are not wrong. They are underdetermined now — correct in intention, missing the mechanism that used to make them automatic. The strongest evidence for this reading is DORA's own, and it cuts bot

An honest question, and the enthusiastic answer is wrong. Each of the six goods has been eroding for decades. Stack Overflow debased the effort proxy long before language models; a copy-pasted answer was never evidence that anyone had reasoned. IDE autocomplete, code generators, scaffolding tools, and frameworks all reduced the cognition per line. Package managers moved the trust boundary years ago — the dependency chosen by something that never read the package name has an ancestor in the developer who never read it either. None of this is new in kind. What is new is conjunction and threshold. The parameter — cost of production — has been falling continuously and smoothly. The system's response has not been smooth. A queue at 60% utilisation absorbing a doubling of arrivals does not degrade twice as much; it crosses into a regime where response time diverges. A codebase whose refactoring share falls from 25% to 20% is fine; the same trend continued to 9.5% removes the homeostat. A trust boundary that leaks occasionally is manageable; one where opening an issue is sufficient is a different security model. This is the ordinary behaviour of systems near a threshold: the driving parameter changes by degree, and the system changes by kind. Water does not become steam gradually. So the correct answer is: Degree in each mechanism. Kind in the conjunction. Nothing here is unprecedented in isolation, and the situation is nonetheless novel, because six thresholds were crossed at once

Part I is finished. Here is the map from what broke to where it gets repaired. Part II builds the apparatus, as four nested rings of control: what the agent sees, what steers it, what it can find, and what it may safely change. Part III assembles the apparatus into a lifecycle with two loops, an autonomy ladder, metrics, and a maturity path. Part IV addresses the humans whose judgment the apparatus exists to concentrate rather than replace. One closing note, because Part I has been relentlessly diagnostic and that is not the whole picture. The free goods are gone and they are not coming back. But re-read §5.3's table, and notice that the gates that survived are the ones you can build more of. A type system, a test, a fitness function, a drift scan: none of these ever depended on effort as evidence, none of them degrades when generation gets cheaper, and all of them get better as the tooling improves. We are not being asked to replace something reliable with something flimsy. We are being asked to replace something implicit and unmeasured with something explicit and measurable — which, for an engineering discipline, is a trade that ought to be welcome. It is simply expensive, and it has to be built on purpose, by someone whose job it is.

Nobody removed six controls: one thing was withdrawn — the price of writing code — and six goods that had been resting on it fell together, which is why the response must be a lifecycle that buys each of them explicitly rather than a tool that cannot supply any of them.

Are there more than six? The list was derived by asking what the cost of production was silently purchasing. That method has no completeness proof, and a good candidate for a seventh is estimation: effort was the basis of every estimate a team ever gave, and if effort no longer correlates with anything, planning may be broken in a way this book does not address. Can a social gate be rebuilt on a non-cost foundation? §5.3 concludes authority must move to computational gates. The alternative — reconstructing review's authority on demonstrated understanding rather than inferred effort — is not obviously impossible, and Chapter 16 gestures at it without solving it. If it can be done, much of Part III becomes simpler. Does the threshold argument in §5.9 survive quantification? The claim that six thresholds were crossed together is qualitative. Each could in principle be given a parameter and a critical value. Nobody has tried, and the exercise would either strengthen the chapter considerably or expose it as a metaphor. What happens at the next order of magnitude? Every argument here concerns generation becoming cheap. If verification becomes comparably cheap — the premise Chapter 8's inferential sensors are betting on — some of these failures reverse. Chapter 27 asks whether that bet is sound.

x: Now the framework, because "more is worse" is not actionable on its own. If more can be worse and less can also be worse, a practitioner needs to know which one they are suffering from. There are exactly two ways a payload fails, and they are opposites. Starvation. The payload lacks information the task requires. The model cannot succeed because the answer is not derivable from what it was given. It will not tell you this; it will guess, plausibly, and the guess will be wrong in a way that looks like reasoning. Signature in Chapter 2's table: 30 lines (14.3%) and no search (15.7%). Dilution. The payload contains everything required, plus a great deal that is not, and the relevant material is no longer reliably attended to. The model has the answer available and does not use it. Signature: the entire file (12.7%), full history (15.0%), iterative search (12.0%). Here is why the framework earns its place: the two failures present almost identically, and the remedies are opposite. In both cases the model produces confidently wrong output. In both cases the obvious diagnosis is "it didn't know enough." A starved model genuinely did not know enough. A diluted model knew perfectly well and did not attend. And because the symptom is the same, the default response to both is the same — add more context — which fixes the first and makes the second worse. t: 6.4 Why the marginal token can be negative
x: The slogan of this chapter has to be earned rather than asserted, so here is the argument. In a bucket, the marginal unit is neutral. Water added to a half-full bucket neither helps nor harms; it simply occupies capacity, and the only failure is overflow. Under that model the correct strategy is obvious: fill it, and worry only when it spills. This is precisely how most teams treat a context window, and it is why "we have a million tokens now" is greeted as the end of the problem. In a budget, items compete, and the constraint is not capacity but what you had to give up. That is closer, but still not right, because a budget's marginal item is at worst worthless. The context payload is worse than a budget. Its marginal item can be negative. An irrelevant token does not merely occupy space; it competes for attention with the relevant ones, adds candidate patterns the model may match against, and dilutes the instruction. Chapter 2 measured the sign: adding true, relevant, on-topic content — the rest of the very file being edited — cost 5.3 points. Once the marginal item can be negative, there is no such thing as a free addition, and therefore no defensible default of "include it in case." Every inclusion is a decision with a cost. That is what makes this engineering rather than configuration. Let me push it one step further, because a decision rule falls out. Or after, detecting what happened and enabling correction — a sensor, feedback. What executes it? A CPU running deterministic code — computational. Or a model producing a probabilistic judgment — inferential. Two clarifications before the argument, because both matter. A mechanism is a vehicle; a cell is a function. A hook is a vehicle — a script that runs at a lifecycle point. It can carry a sensor (run the type checker after every edit) or a guide (inject the current schema before every call). MCP can expose a computational guide (a code graph to query) or reach a sensor (a coverage service). The mapping from tool features to cells is therefore not one-to-one, and I will be careful about that in §7.6 where it matters most. Inferential does not mean inferior. Computational controls are cheap, fast, and reliable but can only check properties expressible in code. "Is this the right abstraction?" and "does this test actually test anything?" are semantic questions, and Chapter 8's hardest problem lives there. The two columns are complements, not competitors, and Böckeler's point is precisely that inferential controls "allow us to both provide rich guidance, and add additional semantic judgment."

x: Here is the distinction that the rest of the chapter turns on, and it is epistemic rather than technical. A guide is an assertion. It says: this is how things should be done here. It is a claim, written in advance, about behaviour that has not happened yet. Its truth is never tested by the act of writing it. A sensor is an observation. It says: this is what did happen. It makes contact with the artefact and returns a verdict about the actual state of the world. The asymmetry between these is the whole game. An assertion can be wrong, stale, contradicted by a neighbouring assertion, or simply ignored, and none of those failures announces itself. An observation can also be wrong — a flaky test, a false-positive lint — but its failures are loud, because a sensor that fires produces an artefact someone must dispose of. Now consider a harness composed almost entirely of guides. It is a system of assertions about the organisation's own behaviour with almost no observation of that behaviour. It will feel well-governed. It will read well in an onboarding document. And it will contain no mechanism by which a false assertion is ever discovered. There is a name for a body of confident claims insulated from contact with evidence, and it is not engineering. Taleb's long argument against narrative — that a coherent story is not a substitute for a record of outcomes, and that coherence is easier to manufacture than accuracy — applies directly. Böckeler states it plainly, and the sentence deserves to be memorised: "Whenever an issue happens multiple times, the feedforward and feedback controls should be improved to make the issue less probable to occur in the future, or even prevent it." Ashby lets us say what harnessability is, rather than merely listing its symptoms: Harnessability is variety reduction already banked. A strongly typed codebase has spent past effort making most programs unexpressible. A codebase with enforced layering has already forbidden most call graphs. That work is done; the regulator now has less to regulate. This reframing has teeth, because it makes harnessability an asset with a balance rather than a vague quality. A team inheriting a well-structured codebase inherits accumulated variety reduction and can build a comprehensive harness cheaply. A team inheriting an untyped, unlayered codebase has no balance to draw on, and must either spend to create some or accept that comprehensive harnessing is unreachable. Which produces Böckeler's inversion, and it is the cruellest sentence in the field: "the harness is most needed where it is hardest to build." Chapter 24 is devoted to this. t: 8.7 Why generated tests cannot be a specification harness
x: The circularity deserves precise statement rather than a warning, because being precise about it reveals what generated tests are good for — which is a great deal. The distinction that falls out is clean and, as far as I can find, not stated anywhere: AI-generated tests are a regression harness, not a specification harness. They detect future divergence from today's behaviour. They cannot detect today's divergence from what was wanted, because they were derived from the same model of intent as the behaviour itself. This is not a dismissal — it is a scoping, and the scope is genuinely valuable. A regression harness protects against Chapter 4's accumulation, catches the cascade when a later change breaks an earlier assumption, and lets an agent self-correct in-loop at Chapter 7's level 2. Generated tests do all of that well and cheaply. What they cannot do is tell you the feature was right in the first place. Which is exactly the failure class Böckeler lists as caught by neither column: misdiagnosis of the underlying problem, over-engineering, unrequested features, and correctness against an intent that was never clearly specified. All four are failures where code and tests agree perfectly. And it explains a phenomenon every reader will recognise: a pull request with comprehensive passing tests, reviewed and merged, that turns out to have solved the wrong problem. Nothing malfunctioned. The harness did its job. Its job was consistency.

t: 8.9 The silent sensor, and harness drills
x: Böckeler poses an open question that sounds almost rhetorical and is in fact the deepest problem in the chapter: If a sensor never fires, is that quality or blindness? By observation of the sensor alone, these two cases are indistinguishable. A test that always passes because the code is correct and a test that always passes because it asserts nothing produce identical output forever. A guide that is followed and a guide that is ignored produce identical artefacts — nothing. A linter misconfigured to check no files reports clean. This is Taleb's silent evidence in its purest engineering form, and worse than the usual case: absence of failure reports is not merely weak evidence of safety, it is exactly what a broken detector produces. The turkey of Chapter 3 at least had data. A silent sensor manufactures data that looks like safety. So the harness has no way to audit itself, and Chapter 7's third ceiling stands. Böckeler names the missing instrument directly: how do we evaluate harness coverage and quality, analogous to code coverage metrics? The literature lists this as unclaimed. So let me claim it, because the answer already exists in a neighbouring discipline. Code coverage tells you a line was executed. Mutation testing tells you something far stronger: deliberately introduce a defect, and check that a test fails. If no test fails, the mutant survives, and you have learned that your suite does not actually constrain that behaviour — regardless of what coverage claimed. T

Chapter 4 identified the mechanism driving structural decay, and left this chapter a specific debt. An agent needs behaviour that already exists somewhere, slightly differently. x: The instinct is to file graphs under retrieval. That undersells them, and LocAgent's most striking number shows why. Consider how an agent without a graph answers a multi-hop question — find the handler for this route, then the service it calls, then that service's repository, then the tests covering each. LocAgent reports an ≈86% cost reduction against proprietary baselines. That is not an accuracy result; it is a payload result. The graph reduced what had to be in context to answer the question — which is precisely Chapter 6's dilution problem attacked at the root rather than managed after the fact. Chapter 6 called progressive disclosure the only lever that addresses both starvation and dilution, and named this chapter as its realisation. Now the identification can be stated exactly: A code graph is progressive disclosure with a typed index. Carry pointers, not payloads; make the pointers navigable by relationship rather than by string; fetch bodies only when the traversal says they matter. The second LocAgent figure is worth as much as the first. A fine-tuned 32-billion-parameter open model reached results comparable to state-of-the-art proprietary models on this task. The graph substituted for model scale. That is the SWE-agent result again, in a different key: the environment is a lever with a large coefficient, and here the coefficient was large enough to close a gap between model tiers.

Nodes are the things that exist; edges are the questions you want answered cheaply. The design discipline is to work backwards from the questions. Three notes on that figure. One consequence of §9.6's originated edge deserves its own section, because I have not seen it raised and it is not small. Chapter 5 established that the trust boundary has moved: every artefact an agent reads is potential instruction, and OWASP ranks Agent Goal Hijacking first on the basis that agents cannot reliably distinguish instructions from data C. The canonical vector is issue text, because opening an issue requires no privilege. Now consider a knowledge graph that links issues, pull-request comments, and commit messages to code entities. KGCompass does exactly this; it is a genuinely useful capability, and it improves localisation because issue text often names the right symbols. It also builds a retrieval path from untrusted input to authoritative-seeming output. The general form: a graph that mixes derived and asserted edges launders the provenance of the asserted ones. Structural edges are derived from an AST and are as trustworthy as the compiler. Edges from issue text are as trustworthy as whoever typed the issue. Merging them into one typed result set with one visual grammar destroys precisely the distinction Chapter 11 will argue must be preserved. The mitigation is not to drop the useful edges. It is to keep the distinction in the data: Type every edge by provenance — derived (AST, compiler, test runner) versus asserted (human prose, issue text, external documentation). Graph engineering sits in the quadrant as a computational guide — feedforward, deterministic, acting before generation. Chapter 7's framing that graph engineering is feedforward guidance made computational is right, and §9.4 adds the reason it matters: computational guides are derived, and derived guidance does not age. Its ceiling is the same one Chapter 6 hit, one level out. A graph answers where and what. It reduces the payload needed to answer relational questions, and it converts an unbounded retrieval problem into a bounded traversal. What it does not do is reduce the amount of structure there is to traverse. A graph over a codebase with four hundred modules, mutual dependencies, and no layering will faithfully report a tangle. It makes the tangle navigable; it does not make it small. Which is Chapter 10's move, and the most radical answer in Part II. Rather than describing the structure better or navigating it faster, change the structure so that the context required to modify any module is bounded regardless of the repository's total size. Chapter 8 gave that its theoretical justification: Ashby forces variety reduction, and harnessability is variety reduction already banked. Chapter 10 asks what happens when you bank it deliberately — and, in the most honest section of Part II, admits that the mechanism is compelling and the causal evidence does not yet exist.

A code graph supplies information no model can be trained into rather than compensating for a capability models are acquiring, which is why it is the only form of feedforward guidance that does not age — and why the architectural prose currently filling context files belongs in a derived, queryable, CI-refreshed structure instead.

Does graph tooling flatten Chapter 4's gradient? The chapter's central mechanism predicts that repositories with graph-backed reference tooling show less of the duplication signature than matched repositories without it. This is the cleanest test of Chapter 4's argument and it has not been run. Do code graphs escape the negative GraphRAG result? The AST-derived versus LLM-extracted distinction is the plausible reason they should, and it is an argument rather than a finding. Somebody should run GraphRAG-Bench's methodology on code graphs specifically. What is the freshness cost at scale? RepoGraph and LocAgent report accuracy and inference cost. Neither reports what it costs to keep a graph current across a large monorepo under continuous change, which is the number an engineering leader actually needs. Is the ADR edge buildable? §9.6 argues that module ──decided_by──► ADR is the highest-value underbuilt edge in the graph, on the grounds that it makes why retrievable at the moment of change. It also requires ADRs to exist, be maintained, and be linked — three organisational practices with poor historical adoption. I believe the edge is worth more than the rest of the graph combined and I have no evidence that anyone can sustain it. How much of a graph survives a language migration or a polyglot repository? Every system cited here is demonstrated primarily on Python.

Chapter 6 tried to solve it by designing the payload, and found a ceiling: the whole file scored 12.7% against 18.0% for a window of it. Chapter 9 tried to solve it by making the repository navigable rather than resident, and got real gains — 92.7% file-level localisation, an 86% cost reduction — but hit a ceiling of its own. A graph over four hundred mutually dependent modules with no layering faithfully reports a tangle. It makes the tangle navigable. It does not make it small. This chapter's move is the one nobody reaches for first, because it is the most expensive: change the codebase so that less has to be known. Chapter 8 already supplied the theoretical warrant. Ashby's constraint forces variety reduction — a regulator cannot regulate more variety than it has a model of, so either the harness grows without bound or the space of what may be produced shrinks. c: Chapter 10 — Structural Engineering: Parnas and the Harnessable Codebase
t: 10.2 The property Parnas did not name
x: Parnas's 1972 criterion is one of the most-cited and least-followed results in software engineering. Decompose a system not by the steps of its processing but by information hiding: each module conceals a design decision likely to change, and its interface reveals as little as it can. The benefits he argued for were changeability, independent development, and comprehensibility. All three are about humans — about limiting how much a person must understand and how far a change propagates through a team. Now state information hiding as a formal property rather than a design heuristic: Encapsulation is the guarantee that a module's interface is a complete description of what a client may rely upon. And notice what follows immediately. If that guarantee holds, then a client reasoning only from the interface reasons correctly. Everything relevant is visible; nothing relevant is hidden elsewhere. An agent working through a bounded context window is a client reasoning from a partial view. So: Information hiding is precisely the condition under which local inference is sound. That is the property. Parnas did not name it, and I do not think he could have, because for fifty years it was masked. Humans compensated for leaky abstractions constantly and invisibly — with institutional memory, with a colleague who said "careful, that thing also mutates the cache," with a sense developed over years of which parts of the system lie to you. The epistemic failure was real and it was absorbed by

x: Evans's bounded context is a strategic pattern: divide a domain into semantically consistent parts, each with its own model and vocabulary, and make the boundaries explicit. The observation for our purposes is almost too neat: a bounded context is a natural context-window boundary. Inside one, the vocabulary is consistent, the invariants are local, and the information needed to make a correct change is co-located. Across one, terms mean different things — the Order in fulfilment is not the Order in billing — and an agent that carries assumptions across the boundary is committing exactly Figure 10.1's error at a larger scale. So domain-driven design's most strategic pattern turns out to double as a scoping instrument for delegation: a task that fits inside one bounded context is a task where local inference can be sound. A task that spans two is a task where it cannot be, and which therefore needs either a human or a much more careful decomposition. That is a usable rule, and Chapter 13 uses it: cross-context tasks belong at a lower autonomy level than within-context tasks of the same apparent size, regardless of how many lines they touch.

Chapter 11 — Verification & Security "The allowlist made the attack easier by auto-approving the very commands that could be hijacked through environment variable poisoning." — on CVE-2026-22708, Cursor terminal allowlist bypass C A security control that increased the attack surface, in a product built by people who were paying attention. This is the chapter's subject in one sentence. What you'll learn: Why security is the tractable half of verification, and behaviour the intractable half That your context payload and your attack surface are the same object, audited with different columns Why OWASP now treats prompt injection as a structural flaw rather than a bug Two verified incidents read for mechanism rather than alarm — and what each one's successful fix reveals The distinction that decides which controls survive injection: belief versus capability — and why capabilities must be scoped by effect, never by name Why benchmarks cannot provide security assurance even in principle The claim this chapter defends: injection defeats every control that operates on what an agent believes and cannot defeat controls that bound what an agent can do. Three of Part II's four rings are belief-based and therefore permeable; the fourth — structure, as capability scoping — is the only durable defence. And provenance, the primitive that would let the other three rings defend themselves, is mechanically available and currently discarded.

Chapter 8 left the behaviour harness unsolved and named the reason: you cannot verify correctness against intent that was never articulated. That is a gap in the human, and no apparatus closes it. Security looks like the same shape of problem — proving the absence of something — and it is not. The two differ in a way that matters enormously for where to spend effort: | Behaviour verification | Security verification | The question | Did it do what was wanted? | Was it influenced by something hostile? | What is missing | Knowledge of what was wanted | Knowledge of where the input came from | Where the gap lives | In the human's unstated intent | In the provenance of text | Mechanically recoverable? | No — intent was never written down | Yes — provenance is trackable and we discard it | That asymmetry is the reason this chapter is more optimistic than its subject matter suggests. Behaviour verification requires eliciting something that does not exist. Security verification requires retaining something we already have and throw away: the knowledge that this paragraph came from an issue comment and that one came from the compiler. So: security is the tractable half of verification. It is urgent, it is currently handled badly, and unlike Chapter 8's elephant it is not waiting on a research breakthrough. It is waiting on engineering.

t: 11.5 Belief-based controls fail; capability-based controls hold
x: Generalise the two incidents and Part II reorganises itself. Every control is one of two kinds. Belief-based controls act on what the agent knows, believes, or is told. Guides, rules, principles, instructions, context files, filters on content, prompts that say "never do X." They work by shaping the agent's model of its situation. Capability-based controls act on what the agent can do. Credentials it does not hold, filesystem paths not mounted, network egress denied, tools not registered, an environment from which the secret has been scrubbed. Injection is an attack on belief. It therefore defeats the first category completely and by construction, and cannot touch the second. A poisoned context can make an agent want to exfiltrate credentials. It cannot give the agent credentials it does not have. Now apply that to Part II's four rings, and the result is uncomfortable. That convergence is worth pausing on. t: The refinement: scope by effect, not by name
x: But the Cursor incident forbids a naïve reading, and getting this right is the difference between the principle being useful and being glib. Cursor's allowlist was a capability control, and it failed. Why? Because it scoped by name rather than by effect. git is not a capability. It is a string that resolves, at execution time, to whatever PATH says it resolves to. The control constrained the identifier and left the referent free. A capability control is only as good as the invariance of what it names. Allowlisting git scopes a name. Granting read-only access to a specific repository scopes an effect. The first is defeated by anything that changes resolution — PATH, LD_PRELOAD, aliases, shims, a modified build script. The second is not. Figure 11.3 leaves three rings permeable. That is not inevitable, and the reason they are permeable is a design choice nobody made deliberately: the context payload discards provenance. By the time text reaches the model it is a flat sequence. The system prompt, a file the agent read, the output of a test run, a paragraph from issue #4412, and a fetched web page all arrive in the same undifferentiated stream. The model has no reliable way to know which is which, and the strongest reason it cannot separate instruction from data is that we did not tell it which was which. Tag every segment of the payload with its origin at assembly time, when the origin is known for free. 2. Security failures are tail events. Taleb's distinction is exactly load-bearing: an average is a meaningful summary in Mediocristan, where no single observation dominates the total. Security lives in Extremistan, where one event does. A tool that behaves correctly on 10,000 curated tasks and catastrophically on the 10,001st has a superb benchmark score and an unbounded loss. You cannot sample your way to tail safety. This is not a criticism of any particular benchmark; it is a statement about what sampling can establish. The governance problem, and it is sharper than the literature admits. Accountability in software engineering travelled with authorship. The person who wrote the code owned it, was called when it failed, and carried the reputational consequence. Review added a second name, but authorship was the anchor. Authorship is now machine. So accountability defaults to the next available signal, which is approval — the person who clicked merge. But Chapter 5 demonstrated that approval is precisely the gate whose informational content collapsed. It was a checkpoint by cost; the cost is gone; and Chapter 3 measured reviewers absorbing double the load while batch sizes grew by roughly a third. We have attached responsibility to the weakest remaining signal. The person accountable for an agent-authored change is the person whose ability to evaluate it we have most thoroughly degraded. This is a skin in the game failure in Taleb's precise sense — not an absence of accountability, but a misalignment between who bears the consequence and who holds the decision. And the consequence is predictable: reviewers who cannot genuinely evaluate what they are accountable for will either approve defensively slowly, becoming the bottleneck, or approve nominally, which Chapter 21 calls Review Collapse. The way out is to move accountability off the instance and onto the decisions that actually determine outcomes: This is why Chapter 13's autonomy ladder is a governance instrument and not a maturity poster.

The four rings are built and the fifth concern runs through all of them. Part II has argued that each ring exists because the one inside it saturates, and that each outer ring makes the inner ones cheaper. This chapter adds the adversarial reading: each outer ring is also harder to talk past. Context can be poisoned, guides can be forged, retrieved facts can be laundered — and a capability the agent does not have cannot be argued into existence. Which is the strongest possible endorsement of Chapter 10's ordering. Make it impossible is not merely the cheapest control to own. It is the only one that survives an adversary. Part III now assembles these pillars into a lifecycle: two loops, an autonomy ladder that turns Figure 11.5's governance requirement into an instrument, a metric system that makes harness coverage and drill results measurable, a maturity path, and an argument about who in an organisation owns any of it.

Injection defeats every control that operates on what an agent believes and cannot defeat one that bounds what an agent can do — so the durable defence is capability scoped by effect rather than by name, and the primitive that would let the other three rings defend themselves is provenance, which is free at assembly time and thrown away before the call.

Can provenance markers be made unspoofable? §11.6's proposal is straightforward except for step four, which may need architectural support rather than prompt convention. This is the highest-value unsolved problem in agentic security and it is an engineering problem, not a research mystery. What is the right trust-level algebra? If payload segments carry trust levels, the harness needs rules for combining them — may low-trust content inform a decision it may not authorise? Does trust propagate through summarisation? Nobody has specified this. How do you audit which controls were in force? Figure 11.5 assigns accountability to the autonomy decision and the harness. Reconstructing after an incident which controls were active, at which versions, requires provenance over the harness as well as over the payload. Is there a security analogue of harness coverage? §11.8 proposes coverage over the read set. That is measurable and better than nothing, and it is not assurance, because the surface is adversarial and open. Does the read set shrink as tooling matures, or grow? MCP, subagents, and web fetch all expand it. Every capability added to an agent adds to the surface an attacker can reach through, and no one is tracking the aggregate.

Chapter 12 — The ADLC Model SDLC's feedback loop returns to requirements. ADLC's feedback loop returns to the harness. What you'll learn: Why a process model earns its place by what it forbids, and the seven prohibitions this one carries Why there must be two loops, and the specific reason: the harness stopped being free and became an artefact The inner loop as a variety funnel — and the diagnostic that follows, which is that surprise at the output is never a fact about the model The flaw in my own model: a monthly outer loop cannot regulate a machine-speed inner one Why a lifecycle without artefacts has no outer loop at all, and therefore fixes instances forever The two ladders — specification strength and agent authority — and why they are orthogonal The claim this chapter defends: ADLC needs a second loop whose subject is the control system rather than the product, because the controls that used to arrive free with the cost of code are now engineered artefacts, and engineered artefacts require their own lifecycle. That loop must run substantially mechanised, because a regulator sampling a thousand times slower than its plant does not regulate it.

The double loop is borrowed, and the borrowing should be explicit. Argyris and Schön distinguished single-loop learning — detecting an error and correcting action within existing assumptions — from double-loop learning, which questions the governing assumptions themselves. That distinction is theirs, and it is exactly the right shape here. But the interesting question is not whether double loops are good in general. It is why software engineering managed for fifty years with essentially one. SDLC has a feedback loop and it returns to requirements. Agile shortened it. DevOps automated the path from decision to production. Every variant closes the loop on the product: build, learn, adjust what you build. None of them needed a loop for the control system, and Chapter 5 explains why. The controls were not artefacts. Scrutiny arrived free with the cost of producing a change. Intent was carried by a person who could be asked. Pacing was free because change was slow. Structural correction happened because somebody eventually found the duplication unpleasant. You do not need a maintenance lifecycle for something you are not maintaining. That is the whole justification for the second loop, and it is worth stating as plainly as possible: The outer loop exists because the harness became an artefact. The two loops in Figure 12.1 touch at exactly one place, and it is easy to miss. The outer loop's input is the inner loop's artefacts. Retrieval traces, execution traces, sensor reports, escalations, recurrence counts. That is the entirety of what the steering cycle has to work with. State it as a consequence: A lifecycle without artefacts has no outer loop. Not a weak one — none. The steering cycle's only inputs are the inner cycle's records, so a team that does not capture them cannot detect recurrence, cannot tell a working control from a silent one, and cannot know whether a failure was starvation or dilution. It will therefore fix instances forever, correctly, one at a time, while the generator remains exactly as likely to produce the next one. This is Taleb's silent evidence in a process diagram. The team sees the defects it fixed. It does not see the pattern across them, because nothing recorded the pattern. And the absence is invisible: an organisation with no traces does not experience a shortage of data. It experiences a series of individually reasonable debugging sessions. Which makes trace capture the cheapest high-value investment in Part III. It buys nothing on its own — no defect is prevented by a log — and it is the precondition for every measurement in Chapter 14 and every control in Chapter 8.

One clarification before Chapter 13, because there is a competing framework that deserves engagement rather than dismissal. Farrag's specification-driven governance proposes an escalating ladder: post-hoc review → natural-language specification → executable contract → constitutional governance, grounded in transaction cost economics B. It is a good ladder and it is measuring something real. It is also not the same axis as Chapter 13's autonomy ladder, and conflating them causes trouble. One is about how strongly the work is specified; the other is about how much authority the agent holds. They are orthogonal, and the two-dimensional space they define is more useful than either alone. The upper-left quadrant — high authority, weak specification — is precisely what Chapter 22 will call mode confusion: vibe coding's operating point applied to production stakes. The lower-right is the failure nobody warns about, because it looks responsible: heavy specification apparatus around work the team will not actually delegate. Chapter 13 develops the vertical axis and gives it a scoring instrument. The horizontal axis is Farrag's, credited, and the pairing is this chapter's contribution: autonomy is only safe to the extent that specification strength has kept pace with it. Prohibition 5 is that sentence in imperative form.

The outer loop exists because the harness stopped being free and became an artefact, and it must run substantially mechanised — because a regulator sampling a thousand times slower than its plant is not a regulator but a historian.

What is the right outer-loop cadence for each phase? §12.7 argues Observe must be machine-paced and Govern human-paced. Where Steer belongs is genuinely unclear, and the answer probably depends on whether the control being installed is computational or inferential. Is the six-phase inner loop the right decomposition? The forced-ordering test of §12.1 is satisfied for Intent-before-Generate and Verify-before-Integrate. It is not obviously satisfied for Ground-before-Decompose — an agent might reasonably decompose first and ground each subtask separately, and I do not know which is better. Can recurrence be detected reliably? Prohibition 3 and Chapter 8's loop both trigger on "this has happened before," which requires classifying failures into modes across sessions. That is a clustering problem over execution traces and nobody has published a method. Does the funnel in Figure 12.2 hold when tasks are long-horizon? Everything here assumes a task with a completion condition reached in minutes to hours. For a multi-day migration the phases interleave, and the variety funnel may reopen partway through. What is the minimum viable artefact set? §12.8 argues artefacts are the only connection between the loops, which makes their absence fatal. It does not say which of the five are load-bearing, and a team cannot capture everything.

Chapter 13 — The Autonomy Ladder An autonomy level enforced by instruction is not an autonomy level. It is a hope with a number attached. What you'll learn: The five levels, defined as sets of revoked capabilities rather than sets of permissions The two inputs that set the ceiling — harnessability and blast radius — and a scoring instrument you can run on your own repositories this week Why the top of the ladder is currently closed for most work, and why the field's marketing suggests otherwise The one class of work where A4 is available today, which turns out to be the outer loop's own maintenance Taleb's barbell applied to autonomy, and the honest account of where the analogy fails The claim this chapter defends: autonomy level is a function of harnessability × blast radius and never of enthusiasm — but the ladder is only real if each level is implemented as capabilities the agent does not hold. And because Chapter 8's behaviour harness remains unsolved, the honest ceiling for most work today is a re-founded A2 rather than the A3/A4 the market is selling.

Three arguments from earlier chapters converge on the need for something like this, and it is worth seeing that they are independent. From Ashby. Chapter 8 established that variety reduction is forced: a bounded regulator cannot govern an unbounded generator, so the space of what may be produced must be narrowed. An autonomy level is variety reduction by scope of authority — the crudest and cheapest form available, because it does not require you to understand the work, only to bound it. From governance. Chapter 11 §11.9 showed that accountability once travelled with authorship, that authorship is now machine, and that responsibility therefore defaults to approval — precisely the gate Chapter 5 demonstrated had collapsed. We have attached responsibility to the weakest remaining signal. The way out is to move accountability onto the decision that actually determines outcomes: this class of change may run at this level of authority. That is a decision someone made, can be asked about, and can revise after an incident. "The reviewer approved it" is not. From economics. Chapter 3 established that verification capacity is the constraint. Autonomy level is the dial that sets how much verification each unit of work consumes. Setting it uniformly across all work — which is what almost every organisation does implicitly — means spending the same scarce resource on a documentation fix and a payments change. So the ladder is not a maturity poster. It is a governance instrument, and Chap

A poisoned context can make an agent want to merge without review; it cannot give the agent merge permission it does not hold. Apply that here and a common practice collapses. A level is real when it is implemented as capabilities the agent does not hold: Notice what this is, structurally. It is via negativa again — defining a level by what is removed rather than what is granted. That makes four appearances now: Chapter 2's shrinking harness, Chapter 8's variety reduction, Chapter 10's unrepresentable states, and now this. The repetition is not stylistic. In a system whose failure modes are unbounded, removal is the only intervention whose effect you can be certain about, so every durable control in this book ends up being subtractive. The rule, stated once: autonomy ceiling = f(harnessability, blast radius). Never enthusiasm, never seniority of the requester, never how well the last task went. Harnessability is Chapter 8's definition: variety reduction already banked. How much of the work of constraining this codebase has already been done? It is an inherited asset with a balance, and it determines how much of the verification you can mechanise. Blast radius is the scope of harm reachable from a change. Chapter 11 sharpened it: what an attacker can reach through the agent is what the agent can reach, so blast radius is a security quantity and a reliability quantity simultaneously. The asymmetry between them matters, and it explains why the rule multiplies rather than adds. Harnessability determines how likely you are to catch a bad change. Blast radius determines what it costs if you do not. Risk is the product, and Taleb's objection to reasoning about probability alone applies with force here: in the presence of a large enough blast radius, a small failure probability is not reassuring, because the expected loss is dominated by a term you cannot estimate. Chapter 11 §11.7 made the same argument about benchmarks — you cannot sample your way to tail safety. Hence the practical rule that follows: blast radius vetoes. A high-blast-radius change does not become eligible for high autonomy because your harness is excellent. It becomes eligible for high autonomy when the blast radius has been reduced — by feature

t: 13.8 The barbell, and where it fails
x: Taleb's barbell strategy is the recommendation to avoid medium risk entirely: hold most of your position in maximum safety and a small remainder in maximally convex bets, rather than spreading everything across a middle whose downside you cannot estimate. In fat-tailed domains it dominates naive diversification. The temptation is to transfer it directly — put the critical decile at A0/A1, the throwaway band at A4, and avoid the mushy A2 middle. I flagged this early in the book's development as an original contribution, and testing it properly shows the transfer is partial. It is worth being precise about which half survives. What transfers. The objection to uniformity. A single organisational autonomy level is exactly the naive-diversification error: it spreads the same medium exposure across work whose blast radii differ by orders of magnitude. And both extremes are correct where they apply — the critical decile belongs at maximum protection regardless of convenience, and the throwaway band belongs at maximum autonomy because its downside is capped by construction and its upside includes both throughput and the outer-loop work of §13.7. What does not transfer. The claim that the middle is worthless. In Taleb's setting, medium-risk positions carry unbounded downside without proportional upside, so avoiding them is free. That is not true here: A2 is where the work is, and Chapter 3's enterprise case measured 2.09× per-capita throughput at essentially A2 B. The middle has real,

t: 13.9 Autonomy creep, and the artefact that stops it
x: Chapter 21 catalogues Autonomy Creep — permission scope expanding by convenience rather than by decision. The mechanism is worth stating here because the remedy belongs to this chapter. Creep does not happen in one step. It happens because each individual expansion is small, plausible, and made under delivery pressure by whoever is blocked. This one time, let it merge without the integration suite — the pipeline is slow and the change is trivial. Nobody decides to move from A2 to A3. The boundary is simply never enforced, and after enough exceptions the exception is the configuration. Two defences, both consequences of earlier chapters. Enforce by capability (§13.3). An expansion that requires granting a permission is an event with a record. An expansion that requires only ignoring an instruction leaves no trace. This is the whole argument for Figure 13.1's revocation column, and it converts creep from a cultural drift into an auditable change. Make the level a policy artefact with an owner and a review date. Chapter 11 §11.9 argued accountability follows the autonomy decision; that requires the decision to exist as a document. Appendix C provides the template; the minimum content is: the class of work, the level, the harnessability and blast-radius scores that justified it, the named owner, the review date, and the conditions that would force a downgrade. That last field is the one everyone omits and the one that matters. A level granted with no stated conditions for revocat

The ladder produces three quantities that a lifecycle needs and that nobody currently measures. Autonomy mix — the distribution of merged work across A0–A4. Chapter 14 makes this a first-class metric, because it is the only number that shows whether delegation is actually happening or whether an organisation has bought agents and kept its old process. Harnessability scores over time — §13.5's instrument, re-run. Rising harnessability is the leading indicator that the ceiling is lifting; it moves before throughput does. Ceiling violations — work that ran above its ceiling. This is Chapter 12's fifth prohibition made countable, and it is the closest thing to a safety metric this book offers. Chapter 14 also inherits the harder problem this chapter has exposed. Everything above depends on knowing the blast radius of a change before it is made, which is a classification problem nobody has automated. Today the scoring is a conversation. It should be a query against Chapter 9's graph — does this change path reach a credential, mutate production data, or cross a bounded context? — and that is a buildable thing that does not exist.

Autonomy is a ceiling set by harnessability × blast radius, implemented as capabilities the agent does not hold — and because the behaviour harness remains unsolved, the honest ceiling for ordinary feature work is a re-founded A2, while the top of the ladder is available today only for the near-zero-blast-radius work that the outer loop needs done anyway.

Can blast radius be computed? §13.10's query is the highest-value missing tool in Part III: reachability of secrets, production data mutation, fan-in, and context-crossing are all graph questions, and answering them automatically would turn a conversation into a gate. Are the weights in §13.5 right? They are judgment. H2 and H4 are weighted equally with H1 and H3, and I suspect the acceptance set and blocking sensors matter more than the rest combined. Somebody with incident data could fit this properly. Does the ceiling matrix survive contact with incidents? Figure 13.2 is derived from argument, not from outcome data. The test is whether organisations that operated above their computed ceiling had more incidents — checkable retrospectively by anyone with both a policy and an incident log. What is the right size of the convex end? §13.8 suggests 20–30% of work qualifies for A4 today. That figure is an estimate from the categories in §13.7, not a measurement, and it will vary enormously by codebase. Does a re-founded A2 actually restore review? The claim is that a held-out acceptance set plus blocking sensors turns full review into review-by-exception. Whether reviewers' effective scrutiny recovers, or whether they simply trust the sensors and skim anyway, is an empirical question about human behaviour that Chapter 19 is better placed to worry about.

Chapter 14 — Metrics for Delegation Report the horizon with the metric, or the metric is not a claim. What you'll learn: The four things a metric must have before it earns a place on a dashboard How to measure the constraint itself — review utilisation — without counting anything you cannot count Why enlarging batches is a false relief valve: it leaves utilisation unchanged and destroys reviewability, derived rather than asserted Harness coverage, and the honest limit of what it measures Why a dashboard with mixed horizons lies by juxtaposition The seven things not to measure, and what each one corrupts The claim this chapter defends: the primary metric of a delegating organisation is not throughput but utilisation of the constraint, and it is measurable from queue behaviour rather than from headcount arithmetic. Everything else is either a guardrail that keeps a count honest, or a measure of whether the steering loop is learning.

Metric chapters fail the same way process chapters do: fifteen plausible indicators, none justified, all gameable, and no team implements more than three. So the standard, applied to every metric below without exception. 1. A decision. Name the choice this number changes. A metric that informs no decision is a report, and reports accumulate until nobody reads any of them. 2. A guardrail. Chapter 3 showed the mechanism precisely: an enterprise hit its target of merged pull requests per engineer while average pull-request size grew by roughly a third B. Nobody gamed anything. The metric was met honestly, and meeting it honestly required the batch growth that made the underlying goal harder. A count is not a measure unless its unit is fixed, so every count in this chapter is paired with the guardrail that holds its unit still. 3. A window. Chapter 3 established that "no quality penalty" means nothing without "measured over twelve months on merge and revert rates," and Chapter 4 showed the acute and chronic proxies disagree because they sample different horizons. Every metric here carries a window, and §14.8 explains why mixing them on one screen is actively harmful. 4. A stated gaming mode. Goodhart's law is not a risk to be managed; it is a certainty to be pre-empted. If you cannot say how a metric will be corrupted, you have not understood it well enough to publish it.

First, what does not change. Chapter 5 §5.8 argued that ADLC contains DevOps rather than replacing it, and DORA's own 2025 finding is the evidence: AI is an amplifier, and the seven capabilities determine whether its benefits reach the organisation at all C. That makes the capability base necessary and insufficient — not obsolete. So deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore stay. Two of them matter more than before: Change failure rate, because DORA 2025 found AI adoption raising throughput and delivery instability simultaneously. This is the metric on which the trade shows up. Lead time for changes, because §14.3 uses its decomposition to measure the constraint. Anyone selling ADLC as a replacement for the four keys is selling something this book does not endorse. What follows is additive.

Chapter 3 established that verification capacity is the binding constraint, modelled the team boundary as a queue, and then admitted a gap: the account was "a model fitted to reported symptoms, not an estimate from instrumented queues," and that nobody has published review utilisation as a first-class metric. This section pays that debt. The quantity of interest is ρ = λ/μ: arrival rate of review-demanding work over review service capacity. As ρ approaches 1, time in system diverges, which is why "we doubled output" and "delivery did not improve" are the same sentence. The obvious approach — count arrivals, estimate capacity from headcount and hours — fails immediately. Reviewer capacity is not headcount × hours; it is the rate at which reviews can be completed at adequate quality, and adequate quality is exactly the thing that silently degrades under load. Any μ you compute from staffing is a fiction that assumes away the phenomenon you are trying to detect. So do not measure ρ directly. Infer it from the queue's behaviour, which is observable. The signature of an approaching saturation point is not that waits are long. It is that waits respond disproportionately to arrivals. Below the knee, a 20% increase in arrivals produces roughly a 20% increase in waiting. Near the knee, the same 20% produces 60% or 100% or more, because the queue's response is convex. Definition. t: 14.4 Batching is a false relief valve
x: Chapter 3 listed four responses to a saturating queue, and observed that a real enterprise pulled two of them: it enlarged batches and it mechanised review. The first deserves an analysis it did not get there, because the result is stronger than "big pull requests are hard to review." Take utilisation ρ = λ/μ, where μ is measured in the same units as λ — items per unit time. Now halve the number of pull requests by doubling their size. λ halves. Fewer items arrive. Service time per item roughly doubles. So μ, in items per unit time, roughly halves. ρ = λ/μ is unchanged. Batching does nothing to utilisation and everything to reviewability. It feels like relief because the queue is visibly shorter, and the queue is shorter because each item is bigger. Two consequences. This is why small batches is a capability rather than a preference. DORA identifies working in small batches among the seven capabilities that determine whether AI's benefits reach the organisation C — an empirical correlation. Figure 14.2 supplies the mechanism: batching is the intuitive response to queue pressure, it does not work, and it costs reviewability, which is the thing under pressure. A team that batches under load has taken the one action that looks like relief and provides none. And it constrains how the Chapter 3 evidence should be read. This is the family the field does not have, and Chapter 8 named its absence as an open problem in the literature — how do we evaluate harness coverage and quality, analogous to code coverage metrics? Harness coverage. Chapter 8 also supplied the constraint that makes it real rather than vain: Harness coverage = known recurring failure modes with a control that has demonstrably fired in a drill within the review window ÷ known recurring failure modes. The phrase demonstrably fired is doing all the work. Without drills, coverage degenerates into a count of configuration entries — the number of rules in a context file — which measures effort rather than effect and is exactly the vanity metric Chapter 8 warned against. A control that has never been shown to fire is Böckeler's silent sensor, and by observation it is indistinguishable from an absent one. And now the honest limit, which I would rather state than have discovered: Harness coverage measures diligence, not safety. The denominator is known failure modes — the ones you have already met. It is silent about everything you have not yet encountered, and it can read 100% while you are fully exposed to a class of failure nobody has imagined. That is Taleb's silent evidence in a denominator. Coverage tells you whether you acted on what you learned. It cannot tell you what you have not learned, and any organisation treating a high coverage figure as assurance has made exactly the error Chapter 11 §11.7 identified about benchmarks

Three, and they are the ones that survive contact with a finance function. Cost per accepted change = (tokens + compute + human review minutes) ÷ changes merged without rework. The denominator is deliberate: changes that were merged and then reworked within 14 days are not accepted, they are deferred. Decision: is delegation economic for this class of work? Gaming mode: excluding review minutes, which is the dominant term and the hardest to instrument. Window: monthly. Review load per engineer per week — hours spent reviewing, per person. Chapter 3 identified this as the true capacity constraint, and the enterprise study measured per-reviewer load roughly doubling B. Decision: staffing, and whether valve 4 is working. Gaming mode: load falls because reviews became nominal, so pair with the same scrutiny proxy as §14.3. Window: weekly, trended quarterly. Context efficiency = tokens consumed per accepted change. This is Chapter 6's budget made measurable, and it has a property most cost metrics lack: it moves in the right direction for two different good reasons. It falls when the payload gets better curated (Chapter 6's dilution reduced) and it falls when the graph replaces exploratory search — LocAgent reported an ≈86% cost reduction from exactly that substitution B. Decision: whether Ground is working. Gaming mode: cheaper models, so hold model constant or normalise. Window: monthly.

The first two are Chapter 4's chronic proxies; the third is §14.4's false-relief-valve indicator and the unit-stability guard for everything else. Each needs a threshold and an owner, or it is a chart. The threshold does not need to be principled — "if duplication rises for two consecutive quarters, the platform team opens an investigation" is a perfectly good rule and vastly better than watching. Now the design problem nobody names. This is Chapter 3's turkey problem in dashboard form. Nobody implements twenty metrics. Here is the set I would start with, chosen so that each is cheap to instrument and none is a vanity number. Two implementation notes that determine whether this works. Metric 5 requires failure-mode labels, and that is the genuinely hard part of this chapter. Chapter 12 §12.7 argued recurrence detection must be automatic, and Chapter 12's open questions conceded that classifying failures into modes across sessions is a clustering problem over execution traces with no published method. Until that exists, time-to-control is measured by hand on a sample — which is worth doing, because a hand-measured median from twenty incidents is enormously more informative than nothing. All five depend on Chapter 12 §12.8's artefacts. A team that does not capture traces, sensor reports, and escalations cannot compute any of them. This is why that section called trace capture the cheapest high-value investment in Part III: it prevents no defect on its own and every measurement here is downstream of it.

Measure the constraint rather than the output: utilisation is unobservable but its consequence is not, so track the elasticity of review wait to arrivals — and remember that enlarging batches leaves that utilisation exactly where it was while destroying the reviewability it was supposed to protect.

Can failure modes be classified automatically? Time-to-control, harness coverage, and Chapter 8's steering trigger all depend on recognising "this has happened before" across sessions. It is a clustering problem over execution traces, and it is the single most valuable missing tool in Part III. What is a good harness coverage figure? §14.6 defines the measurement and cannot supply a target. Nobody knows whether 40% is negligent or excellent, and the denominator's dependence on known failure modes may make cross-organisation comparison meaningless. Is the elasticity threshold right? The bands in Figure 14.1 — below 1 slack, 1–2 loading, above 3 the cliff — are reasoned from queue behaviour, not fitted to data. Anyone with two years of review telemetry could calibrate them properly in an afternoon. Does W-as-wait survive automated review? Chapter 3's enterprise study had bots performing roughly 38% of review events and half of all comments, and set its own boundary at the first human review for exactly this reason. As automated review grows, "first human review" may stop being a meaningful event, and the constraint metric would need redefining around it. Can blast radius be computed? Inherited unresolved from Chapter 13. Ceiling violations — arguably the closest thing to a safety metric here — cannot be counted until it is.
