Chapter 15 — The Maturity Model Most organisations have the one level that is not a prerequisite for anything. What you'll learn: The five requirements a maturity model must meet before it is anything but a sales instrument Why maturity is which feedback loops are closed, not how much apparatus is installed The five levels, and the evidence for where teams actually sit The flaw in the conventional ordering: it is sorted by cost of adoption, not by dependency — which is why everyone is stuck at the same rung The prerequisite no maturity model mentions and nothing above it works without What does not improve as you climb, which is most of what matters The claim this chapter defends: the standard progression is ordered by what is cheap rather than by what is necessary. Level 1 is where almost everyone is, and it is the only level that is not a precondition for any other — so the useful move for most teams is not to perfect it but to leave it, sideways, for the two things that actually unlock the rest.

t: 15.1 What a maturity model must earn
x: Maturity models have a poor reputation and have earned it. They are typically unfalsifiable, linear about things that are not, self-assessed, aspirational at the top with no evidence anyone is there, and — most damningly — structured so that the answer to every level is to buy something. So, as with Chapter 12's process model and Chapter 14's metrics, the standard first. 1. Observable from artefacts. If a level can only be established by asking someone how they work, it is a survey. Each level below has an artefact test — something you can look at. 2. Ordered by dependency, not ambition. Level n+1 must be genuinely difficult or impossible without level n. Otherwise the model is a list wearing a staircase. 3. An honest distribution. Where do organisations actually sit, with evidence? A model whose levels are all thinly populated at the top is describing an aspiration, and should say so. 4. A stated cost per level. The point of the model is deciding whether to climb. Without cost, it is exhortation. 5. A statement of what does not improve. The via negativa requirement, and the one that separates an honest model from a sales instrument. §15.8 is that section, and it is longer than one might hope. Requirement 2 is where the conventional version of this model fails, and §15.5 is about that.

t: 15.2 Maturity is which loops are closed
x: The first design decision: what is being measured? The tempting answer is apparatus — how many controls, how many rules, how much configuration. It is tempting because it is countable, and it is wrong for two reasons already established. Chapter 2 and Chapter 8 showed the apparatus should shrink. Harness mass measures what the model cannot yet do for itself; the optimal harness gets smaller as models improve, and Chapter 8 added the retirement arm to make that operational. An organisation with fewer controls than last year may be more mature, not less. Any model that counts apparatus punishes exactly the behaviour it should reward. And counting apparatus is the definition of Harness Theatre. Chapter 14 §14.9 puts "count of rules, skills, or context-file entries" on the do-not-measure list for precisely this reason: it measures effort rather than effect. The better criterion: Maturity is which feedback loops are closed. This works because a closed loop leaves evidence that cannot be faked. A control installed in response to a recurrence has a date, a named failure mode, and a prior incident it points back to. You can look at it. You cannot manufacture that record by writing more configuration, which is exactly the property requirement 1 demands. Level | The loop that is closed | L0 | None. Individual sessions, nothing shared. | L1 | None. Context is shared but nothing observes whether it works. | L2 | The inner loop closes. Sensors fire during the work and the agent self-corre

| Level | Signature | Artefact test | L0 | Ad hoc | Individuals use assistants; no shared configuration; no policy | Nothing in version control governs agent behaviour | L1 | Configured | Shared context files, conventions written down, version-controlled | An AGENTS.md or equivalent exists and has been edited more than once | L2 | Sensed | Blocking computational sensors inside the agent's edit cycle; execution traces captured; small batches enforced; review by exception begins | A hook configuration exists and a store of execution traces exists | L3 | Steered | Recurrence produces controls; controls are dated and attributed; retirement happens; graph exposed as a tool | A control whose commit message references the prior incidents that motivated it — and a control that was removed, with a reason | L4 | Templated | Harness templates per service topology; autonomy governed by written policy; harness coverage drilled and measured | A harness template consumed by a service its authors did not write | The artefact tests are the useful column. Each is a thing you can go and look for this afternoon, and each is hard to produce without genuinely being at that level. Two are worth dwelling on. L3's test requires a removal. A team that only ever adds controls has an install arm and no retirement arm, which Chapter 8 §8.2 showed terminates in theatre. The deleted control with a stated reason is the cheapest available evidence that the loop runs in both directions, and in my experience i

Requirement 3, and this is where the model stops being aspirational and becomes a description. From the 2,853-repository study A: The authors' own summary is the one-line version: "Harness engineering in open source today is therefore mostly context engineering." Two caveats that matter. This is open source, and the authors say plainly that enterprise practice may differ. And it is a point-in-time snapshot of a field whose conventions are still consolidating — their words. But the one enterprise case we have in detail points the same way: the organisation in Chapter 3 reached automated review under queue pressure, which is a partial L2 move, and did it without naming it, measuring it, or deciding how much to trust it B — which is L2 apparatus without an L3 loop. So the honest statement: essentially the whole field is at L1, with a thin tail into L2 and almost nothing above. Levels 2–4 are aspirational, and a book that presented them as a normal progression would be describing a world that does not exist.

Now the part that matters, and it starts with a question the conventional model does not ask. Why is everyone at L1? The comfortable answer is that L1 is the foundation — you must write your conventions down before you can enforce them, so of course adoption starts there. It is a satisfying story and I do not think it is true. Test it against requirement 2. Is L2 genuinely difficult or impossible without L1? Consider what an L2 move actually requires: a hook that runs your type checker on every agent edit and refuses the edit if it fails. What does that depend on? An agent loop with a lifecycle hook, and a type checker. It does not depend on a context file. Nothing about the sensor consults AGENTS.md. You could wire a blocking sensor into an agent's edit cycle in a repository with no context file at all, and it would work exactly as well. L1 is not a prerequisite for L2. The dependency does not exist. So why did the field converge on L1? Chapter 7 §7.7 already answered it, and the answer was a cost gradient, not a dependency: Writing a paragraph in a markdown file takes minutes, requires no tooling, breaks nothing, and produces an artefact that looks like progress. Wiring a check into every edit requires deciding what to check, building it, integrating it, and living with its false positives forever. Both are harness work. One costs an afternoon; the other costs a quarter and an owner. The field did the cheap one, universally, and then a maturity narrative formed around the o

Look again at Figure 15.2 and notice the node that appears in no conventional maturity model: trace capture. Chapter 12 §12.8 established why it belongs there. The outer loop's only inputs are the inner loop's artefacts — retrieval traces, execution traces, sensor reports, escalations, recurrence counts. Without them: A lifecycle without artefacts has no outer loop. Not a weak one — none. Which means L3 is unreachable without trace capture, regardless of how many controls exist. A team with excellent sensors and no traces cannot detect recurrence, cannot tell a firing sensor from a silent one, and cannot compute a single one of Chapter 14's five starter metrics. It will fix instances forever, correctly, one at a time. This is why L2 in §15.3 has two components rather than one, and why its artefact test requires both a hook configuration and a trace store. Sensors without traces gets you a better inner loop and a permanently closed door to L3. Traces without sensors gets you an observable inner loop with nothing to observe. They are a pair. And the cost asymmetry is striking. Trace capture prevents no defect on its own — it is pure overhead by any local measure — and it is the precondition for every measurement and every control above it. It is the cheapest high-leverage investment in Part III and it will lose every prioritisation argument it is ever entered into, because its benefit accrues to a loop the organisation has not started running yet.

Requirement 4. Honest orders of magnitude rather than false precision. Level | What it costs | Where the cost falls | L1 | Days. One person, one document, ongoing small edits | The team | L2 | Weeks to a quarter, plus permanent ownership of false positives | A platform or infrastructure owner | L3 | A standing role. Somebody owns the harness, runs drills, and decides what to retire | Named individual, continuous | L4 | A platform team, plus a variety-reduction decision the organisation must actually make | Executive — this is an architecture commitment | The last row is the one people underestimate. L4 is not a tooling investment. Chapter 8 §8.3 established the Ashby constraint: a bounded regulator cannot govern an unbounded generator, so harness templates only work if the organisation has committed to a limited set of service topologies. That is a decision about architectural freedom, and it will be resisted by every team that wants to choose its own stack. A platform group that intends to let every team choose freely and also ship comprehensive harness templates is attempting something Ashby forbids, and no amount of L4 investment resolves it. Two ongoing costs that do not appear in any maturity model and should: False positives are permanent. A blocking sensor that fires wrongly costs attention every time, forever, and someone must own tuning it. Chapter 2's iterative-search result — a well-built capability scoring 12.0% against 15.7% for having no such capability — is the

Requirement 5, and this is the section that decides whether the model is honest. Behaviour verification does not improve. Chapter 8's behaviour harness is unsolved at every level. An L4 organisation still cannot mechanically verify that a feature does what was actually wanted, because generated tests prove consistency rather than correctness and a held-out acceptance set only checks the intent that was written down. Chapter 13 §13.6 drew the consequence: L4 does not license A3 or A4 for ordinary feature work. Specification quality does not improve. Chapter 0's line stands unamended at every level: a harness cannot verify correctness against a requirement never articulated. An L4 organisation with poor specifications produces well-harnessed, thoroughly-tested, efficiently-delivered wrong software — faster than it used to. Chapter 17 — Ten Shifts You are not being asked to become a different kind of engineer. You are being asked to notice that a price changed. What you'll learn: The four tests a "shift" claim must pass before it is content rather than exhortation Why all ten are the same shift observed ten times, and the parameter each traces to The one on the conventional list that is not a shift, and what it is instead Why some shifts happen the moment you read them and others resist for years — a distinction that determines what the rest of Part IV is about What each shift costs, and the reason the costs land on individuals while the benefits do not The claim this chapter defends: every shift here is a behaviour that was correct under the old economics and became incorrect when the price of producing code collapsed. That framing matters, because it means the reader is not being asked to repent of bad habits — they are being asked to re-derive a set of rational responses under a parameter that moved.

t: 17.1 What makes a shift claim content
x: Lists of mindset shifts are cheap. They are typically unfalsifiable, faintly moralising, and structured so that the reader's current behaviour is a character flaw. So, as with Chapter 12's process model, Chapter 14's metrics, and Chapter 15's maturity levels: the standard first. A shift claim is content only if it passes four tests. 1. The old behaviour was correct. This is the decisive one. If the "from" side was always wrong, you are not describing a shift — you are correcting an error, and the honest framing is that people were mistaken. A genuine shift starts from a behaviour that was rational given the conditions, which means the reader was not being foolish. 2. A specific parameter moved. Name it. "Things are different now" is not a mechanism. Each shift below traces to something identifiable that changed, and if it cannot, it does not belong on the list. 3. It is falsifiable. You can state what would show the shift is unnecessary, or that it reverses. 4. It costs something. A free shift is a preference, not a shift. If nobody resists it, it needed no chapter. Test 1 is the one that reorganises everything, and it produces the chapter's structure.

Chapter 5 made the book's central structural argument: software engineering's controls were not designed, they were purchased by the expense of writing code. One pillar silently held up six goods — scrutiny, intent, pacing, a trust boundary, structural homeostasis, and the premise that production was the expensive step. Remove the pillar and all six fail at once. Chapter 5 traced the institutional consequences: which gates stopped carrying information, which assumptions failed. This chapter traces the individual ones. And the ten shifts turn out not to be ten things. That is the claim this chapter rests on, and it is why the tone here is not corrective. Every behaviour on the left-hand side of every shift below was the right answer for as long as producing code was expensive. Engineers are not being asked to abandon bad practice. They are being asked to re-derive good practice under a different price.

t: 17.4 The one that is not a shift
x: Test 1 disqualifies one item on the conventional list, and saying so is the difference between analysis and a slide. Big-bang delivery → small batches is not a shift. Small batches was already correct before agents, and had been for a decade. Continuous integration and continuous delivery made it correct; DORA's research established it empirically long before this book's subject existed. Nobody discovered in 2024 that large batches are bad. What actually changed is the cost of non-compliance, and it rose sharply for a reason Chapter 14 §14.4 derived: batching is the intuitive response to a saturating review queue, and it does not work. Halve the pull-request count by doubling size and arrivals halve, service capacity in items halves, and utilisation is unchanged — while reviewability, blast radius per item, and revert granularity all degrade. So the honest reclassification: not a new shift, but an old one whose penalty for non-compliance became severe. That distinction matters practically. A team that never adopted small batches is not behind on an AI transition; it is behind on a DevOps transition, and Chapter 5 §5.8 established that ADLC contains DevOps rather than replacing it. Three mechanisms for why the belief survives the experience — none of which is a belief The finding that makes introspective calibration impossible rather than merely difficult: the signals that track your performance stop tracking it What trust actually is, once you stop treating it as an attitude Practices that calibrate, and why briefings are not among them The claim this chapter defends: trust is not a belief about output quality but a decision about how much verification to spend, and its calibration should be judged by whether that spend is well allocated. This matters because the introspective route to calibration is not merely biased — under AI assistance the physiological and self-reported signals that normally correlate with performance cease to correlate with it, which means calibration has to be built from external instruments or not at all.

METR's randomised controlled trial gave sixteen experienced developers 246 real tasks in repositories they had worked in for an average of five years A. Before starting, they forecast that AI would make them 24% faster. Measured, AI-allowed tasks took 19% longer — confidence interval +2% to +39%. Afterwards, having lived through it, they estimated AI had made them 20% faster. The third line is the one that matters. The first is a forecast, and forecasts are routinely wrong. The third is a retrospective report about an experience the person just had, and it was wrong by roughly forty percentage points in the same direction as the forecast. METR's own later survey work puts a number on the general case: in early 2025, people overestimated AI's effect on their time spent on tasks by 40 percentage points on average B. And a 2026 survey of 349 technical workers found a median self-reported 1.4–2× change in the value of their work — with METR themselves noting there are reasons to be sceptical of the magnitude, and observing that public estimates from surveys have consistently exceeded those from field experiments and quasi-experiments B. One further datum, and it is the one that should worry anyone setting a budget: nearly 89% of engineering leaders reported that developer productivity improved after adopting AI coding tools B. The overestimation is not confined to the people doing the work. It is larger, and less checkable, one level up — which is precisely where the spending dec

Here is a fact that appears to contradict everything in §18.1. The 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey found developer trust in AI at its lowest recorded level C: 46% actively distrust the accuracy of AI tool output — up sharply from 31% the previous year 33% trust it Only 3% report highly trusting it Among experienced developers, 2.6% highly trust and 20% highly distrust Positive sentiment fell from over 70% in 2023 and 2024 to 60% And 84% use or plan to use these tools anyway, up from 76% So developers are sceptical, increasingly so, and the most experienced are the most sceptical of all. How can a population this distrustful overestimate its own speedup by forty points? The resolution is that these are different judgements about different objects. Trust in accuracy asks: is this output correct? Developers have direct, frequent, immediate evidence on this. They see wrong code, they correct it, and their estimate updates — which is exactly what the rising distrust figure shows. This is a well-calibrated judgement, improving over time, because the feedback loop is tight. Belief about throughput asks: did this whole process take less time than the alternative? The alternative did not happen. There is no feedback loop at all, and §18.3 explains why the substitute signal points the wrong way. The practical warning for anyone running an engineering organisation: "Our engineers are appropriately sceptical" is not protection. Scepticism about output accuracy is orthogonal to calib

t: 18.3 Three mechanisms, none of them a belief
x: Why does the retrospective estimate survive the experience that should have corrected it? One: the felt signal tracks effort; the measure tracks duration. The subjective experience of work is dominated by effortfulness rather than elapsed time. Reading generated code is recognition; writing it is recall, and recall is heavier. So a session composed largely of reading, checking, and correcting feels lighter than one composed of authoring — even when it runs longer on the clock. Section 18.4 is the evidence that this is real and measurable rather than plausible. Two: the counterfactual is unavailable. To know you were slower you would need to know how long the task would have taken otherwise. That world does not exist. So the estimate is not retrieved, it is constructed — and it is constructed from what was salient. The moments the agent produced something impressive are highly salient. The forty minutes spent understanding why its output failed feel like ordinary debugging, which is what work has always felt like, and are not attributed to the tool at all. This is structurally identical to Chapter 4's problem with debt. That chapter showed technical debt is unmeasurable because it is a claim about a codebase that does not exist. Speed estimation fails for the same reason: both require comparison against a counterfactual, and both therefore admit whatever story is most available. Three: waiting is not encoded as working. If introspection is unreliable, the natural next move is to introspect more carefully — to attend to your own effort, notice your own state, and calibrate from the inside with more discipline. There is now evidence that this route is closed. Burelli and colleagues ran a multisite, within-subjects crossover study at two universities — Bari and the IT University of Copenhagen — collecting EEG, eye-tracking, electrodermal activity, and heart-rate variability alongside a rubric-based performance score and NASA-TLX self-reported workload across six dimensions. The study was pre-registered as a Stage 1 Registered Report with In-Principle Acceptance at ESEM 2025, which means the hypotheses were fixed before the data existed B. Two families of finding. First, cognitive engagement fell. Under AI assistance the EEG θ/α ratio was lower during the first task and the gaze blink rate was higher during the second — both, in the authors' words, "consistent with reduced cognitive engagement when developers offload generative effort to the model." This is §18.3's first mechanism, measured neurophysiologically rather than argued: the work genuinely is lighter. Notably, the pattern did not differ between undergraduate and graduate students, which Chapter 20 will have to reckon with. Second — and this is the finding that changes what calibration can mean — the signals stopped tracking performance. Read carefully, this is a stronger claim than "self-report is biased." A biased instrument can be co

Given all that, the standard framing of "calibrated trust" — hold beliefs about reliability that match observed frequencies — is not usable. It asks you to tune an instrument that has been unplugged. So reframe. Ask what trust does rather than what it is. Trust is not a belief about quality. It is a decision about how much verification to spend. That is what trust determines operationally: whether you read the whole diff or skim it, whether you run the tests yourself, whether you check the edge case, whether this change needs a second pair of eyes. Every one of those is an allocation of the scarce resource Chapter 3 identified as the binding constraint. Which yields the definition this book uses: Miscalibrated trust is misallocated verification capacity. The reframing earns its place for a practical reason: an allocation is observable. You cannot see someone's belief about model reliability, and after §18.4 they cannot see it either. You can see how long they spent, what they ran, and what they read. Trust becomes an engineering quantity rather than a psychological one.

t: 18.6 The two errors are not symmetric
x: Standard calibration treats over- and under-confidence as symmetric errors to be minimised. Here they are not, and the asymmetry should be built into policy rather than discovered. Under-trust costs capacity. You verify things that did not need it. The cost is real, linear, and bounded: some hours, spent on the wrong changes. It shows up immediately in Chapter 14's review-load metric. Over-trust costs escapes. Something got through. The cost is unbounded in the tail — Chapter 11 established that security failures are Extremistan, where one event dominates the total, and Chapter 4 established that structural damage arrives late and is hard to attribute. So the loss function is asymmetric, and Taleb's argument applies directly: when one side of an error is bounded and the other has an open tail you cannot estimate, symmetric optimisation is the wrong objective. The correct policy is deliberately biased toward under-trust where blast radius is high, accepting known waste to avoid unbounded exposure. Which is Chapter 13's blast-radius veto arriving from the psychological side rather than the governance side. That chapter said no amount of harness quality makes a severe-blast-radius change eligible for high autonomy; this one says no amount of accumulated good experience should make it eligible for low verification. Two derivations, same rule.

If introspection is closed and briefings do not work — METR's cohort knew the result and still felt fast — what remains? The calibration literature, developed for forecasting rather than for engineering, is unusually clear about this: calibration improves through frequent, recorded, scored predictions with fast feedback, and it does not improve from being told one is miscalibrated. Applied here, three practices, in descending order of value and ascending order of cost. One: the prediction log. Before opening an agent-produced change, record one bit — will this need changes? Then review, and record the outcome. The prediction log works precisely where the throughput estimate fails. The counterfactual problem of §18.3 does not arise, because you are predicting an observable event rather than an alternative history. The feedback is immediate rather than never. And the record is external, which is what §18.4 established is necessary. Two: start from the base rate, not the diff. Chapter 14's first-pass acceptance rate, computed per task class, is your team's base rate. Trust in a specific change should begin there and be adjusted, rather than being constructed fresh from how the diff looks — because how a diff looks is exactly the salience-driven signal §18.3 warned about. This is reference-class forecasting applied to review, and it requires the metric to exist, which is why Chapter 14 comes first. Three: the held-out acceptance set is calibration infrastructure. Chapter 8's part

Trust as allocation (§18.5) is observable. Four proxies, all derivable from artefacts a team already produces if it followed Chapter 12 §12.8: Proxy | What it reveals | Time spent per change, by task class | Where verification capacity is actually going | Whether the reviewer ran the code | Whether trust is being extended past reading | Depth of reading — beyond the summary, into the diff | Whether the review is nominal | Prediction-log hit rate (§18.7) | Direct calibration measurement | One honest caution. Chapter 16 §16.7 rejected attention metrics — time in file, scroll depth — as a way of rebuilding review's authority, on the grounds that they are proxies for effort one layer down and are gameable in an afternoon. The proxies above are the same measurements pointed at a different question, and the objection partly transfers. The difference is the incentive. Nobody has a reason to game "I trusted this" the way they have a reason to game "I reviewed this carefully", because the first is not what they are evaluated on. That difference is real and it is not permanent: the moment these become performance measures, they become worthless. Use them diagnostically, hold them privately, and do not put them in a performance review.

A closing observation that follows from §18.1's least-quoted figure. Nearly 89% of engineering leaders reported productivity improvements from AI coding tools B. Leaders are further from the work, receive their information through reports from people whose own estimates are miscalibrated by forty points, and have less access to any corrective. Their estimate is a summary of summaries, and every step in the chain adds the same directional error. They are also the people who set throughput mandates — and Chapter 12's seventh prohibition forbids exactly that, because generation is the elastic side and mandating it raises arrival rate against fixed capacity. The best-documented enterprise case ran this experiment: a CTO mandate to double productivity, measured in merged pull requests per engineer, which was met while batch size grew by roughly a third B. So the calibration problem is worst where its consequences are largest, and the remedy is the same one this whole chapter argues for. Not better beliefs. Instruments — Chapter 14's five metrics, reported without self-report anywhere in the chain.

Trust is a decision about how much verification to spend, not a belief about quality — and it cannot be calibrated introspectively, because under AI assistance the physiological and self-reported signals that normally track performance stop tracking it, which leaves external instruments as the only route.

Does the decoupling hold for professionals? Burelli et al. studied students; METR's inversion was found in experts. The two fit together well and nobody has closed the gap by running biometrics on experienced developers. This is the most valuable replication in Part IV. Does the prediction log actually calibrate? §18.7 applies a well-established result from forecasting to a domain nobody has tested it in. It is cheap enough that any team could run the experiment in a quarter, and I would like to know if it fails. Does estimation error scale with generation latency? §18.3's third mechanism predicts it should. That is testable with existing telemetry and would distinguish the three mechanisms, which currently all predict the same sign. Is the leadership error additive or multiplicative? §18.9 assumes each reporting layer adds the same directional bias. If it compounds, the figure at board level is worse than 89% suggests and nobody has measured it. Does distrust of accuracy ever transfer to throughput calibration? §18.2 argues the two judgements are independent. If some intervention couples them, it would be worth more than any instrument in §18.7.

Chapter 19 — Cognitive Offloading Confidence in the tool was associated with less critical thinking. Confidence in oneself was associated with more. — Lee et al., Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon, CHI 2025 A 319 knowledge workers · 936 first-hand examples What you'll learn: The paradox Chapter 15 left here: a mature harness works by increasing confidence in the tool, and confidence in the tool is what erodes the faculty the harness cannot replace Three studies, three methods, three populations, one direction — and why the weakest of them is probably an underestimate The two confidences, and the atrophy loop that runs between them The trap created by combining this chapter with the last one An ordering effect with a measurable brain correlate, which is the most actionable finding in Part IV Where judgment relocates, and who in an organisation is permitted to keep it The claim this chapter defends: offloading is real, measurable by three independent methods, and it degrades verification judgment specifically — which is the judgment the lifecycle now asks people to exercise most. The resolution is not to delegate less but to attend to the order of delegation and the maintenance of self-efficacy, because the finding that identifies the problem also identifies the variable that protects against it.

Chapter 15 §15.8 listed what does not improve as harness maturity rises: behaviour verification, specification quality, safety at severe blast radius, and — flagged provisionally, deferred here — human judgment. It stated the difficulty in one sentence and left it: The mechanism that makes Level 4 valuable is the same one that erodes the faculty Level 4 cannot replace. Unfold that. A harness exists to make delegated output trustworthy without a human reading all of it. Chapter 18 showed this is exactly right: review by exception is only real when a sensor is blocking and the reviewer has evidence enough to stop reading what it covers. The whole apparatus of Part II is, functionally, a machine for producing justified confidence in delegated work. And the verified finding at the head of this chapter says confidence in the tool is associated with less critical thinking. So the better your harness, the more warranted your confidence, and the less critical thought you bring to the residue — which is precisely the class of failure Chapter 8 established the harness cannot catch: misdiagnosis of the underlying problem, over-engineering, unrequested features, and correctness against an intent that was never stated. This is not an argument against harnesses. It is an argument that the harness has a side effect on its operator, and that a lifecycle which does not account for it is optimising one term of a two-term problem.

The evidence comes from three studies with almost nothing in common except their sign. Self-report, knowledge workers. Lee and colleagues at Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon surveyed 319 knowledge workers who supplied 936 first-hand examples of generative AI use across IT, design, administration, and finance, published at CHI 2025 A. They assessed six categories of critical thinking — knowledge, understanding, application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation. The headline: generative AI reduces the perceived effort of critical thinking while encouraging over-reliance, and confidence in the tool predicted less critical thinking while self-confidence predicted more. EEG, essay writing. The MIT Media Lab study Your Brain on ChatGPT put 54 participants into three conditions — LLM, search engine, and unaided — while writing essays, and measured neural connectivity B. Unaided writers showed the strongest and most widespread networks across all frequency bands. Search-engine users sat between 34% and 48% lower. LLM users showed up to 55% less neural communication in frequencies associated with deep thinking and internal monitoring. The authors coin cognitive debt for the resulting state, and report shallow encoding and poor recall: participants had not internalised essays they had produced. EEG, eye-tracking, EDA and HRV, programming. Burelli and colleagues, from Chapter 18: EEG θ/α ratio lower and gaze blink rate higher under AI assistance, "consistent with reduced cognitive

The most useful thing in Lee et al. is not that critical thinking declines. It is which variable predicts the decline. Confidence in the tool → less critical thinking Confidence in oneself → more critical thinking These are separable, and that separation is the whole of this chapter's practical content. It means the intervention is not "trust the tool less" — a thing Chapter 18 showed is already true and does not help, since developers report historically low trust while still overestimating throughput by forty points. The intervention is on the other variable. But the two are coupled by a loop, and the loop runs the wrong way. The left-hand loop is the atrophy cycle and it is self-reinforcing. The right-hand path is not a cycle — it is a one-time cost of the harness doing its job, and it is the cost Chapter 15 said maturity cannot avoid. This distinction matters for intervention. You cannot break the right-hand path without giving up the harness. You can break the left-hand loop, and §19.7 is about how.

Lee et al.'s second finding is a description of the job rather than of the worker. The nature of knowledge work under generative AI shifts along two axes: From | To | Information gathering | Information verification | Problem solving | Response integration | Or, in the phrasing that circulated widely and is accurate enough to use: knowledge workers become AI output verifiers rather than problem solvers. Chapter 12's inner loop is the same claim in process form. Generate is delegated; Verify and Integrate are what remain human. Chapter 5 §5.5 put it structurally: human judgment relocates rightward and upward — to the specification before generation and to the harness that governs a class of changes, rather than to each instance. So far, consistent. But putting Lee's shift next to Chapter 18's central finding produces something neither says on its own.

Chapter 18 established, from a pre-registered study with physiological measurement, that under AI assistance the internal signals which normally track performance stop tracking it: electrodermal activity correlated with performance in the non-AI condition and not in the AI condition, and of six self-reported workload dimensions only one showed the same asymmetric pattern. Chapter 19 establishes that the work is becoming predominantly verification. Put them together. That is the trap, and I do not think it has been stated. Each of the three findings is modest on its own. Together they describe a situation in which the single faculty the lifecycle depends on most is the one least able to tell how well it is doing, and least exercised. It also explains something otherwise puzzling in Chapter 3's evidence: why merge and revert rates stayed flat while reviewers absorbed double the load. If verification judgment is degrading slowly and its self-assessment signal is broken, the degradation would be invisible in exactly the short-horizon proxies that stayed flat. That is not proof of degradation. It is a warning that the measurement that reassured us is silent on this question.

Now the resolution, and it requires a distinction the studies do not make. "Judgment" is not one faculty. At least two are in play here, and they are affected differently. Verification judgment — is this output correct, complete, and appropriate? This is exercised on generated artefacts, its feedback signal is decoupled (Chapter 18), and it is the one the atrophy loop attacks, because the practice that built it was writing the code yourself and finding out where you were wrong. Specification judgment — what should be built, what must not break, what constraint is load-bearing, when not to delegate at all. This is exercised before generation. Chapter 12's variety funnel showed that phases 1–3 are where variety is reduced, and Chapter 0 named specification as the last human monopoly. The lifecycle in Part III already relocates human attention toward the second. Chapter 12 made Intent a phase with an artefact rather than an assumed precondition; Chapter 8's held-out acceptance set requires a human to state acceptance before generation exists. So the paradox has a partial resolution: Delegation degrades verification judgment and can leave specification judgment intact — because specification judgment is exercised on a problem rather than on an output, and the problem does not get delegated. Partial, because of a question this chapter cannot answer and Chapter 20 must: can you specify well if you never verified deeply? The intuition about what will break, which constraint is load-

The most actionable finding in Part IV is an ordering effect, and it comes from the MIT study's crossover condition. Participants who wrote unaided first and used the LLM afterwards — the brain-to-LLM group — showed higher memory recall and activation of occipito-parietal and prefrontal regions, comparable to search-engine users. The reverse ordering did not produce that. This is worth more than any exhortation about mindful AI use, because it is cheap, specific, and has a measured brain correlate. And it maps onto something Chapter 18 already recommended for a different reason: the prediction log — recording will this need changes? before opening the diff — is brain-before-LLM applied to review. You form your own judgment first. Chapter 18 proposed it to calibrate trust; it turns out to also be the practice that keeps the faculty alive. Two habits do the same work. Attempt before delegating, on anything you intend to stay good at. Not everything — that would forfeit the benefit entirely. This is a deliberate allocation: pick the competences you need to retain and pay the minutes on those. Maintain self-efficacy deliberately. Lee et al. identifies self-confidence as the protective variable, so the organisational move is anything that builds genuine competence rather than anything that reduces tool use. Chapter 20 takes this up as a training problem. And one that is more contested but worth stating. Aviation human-factors practice responded to automation dependency in part by

t: 19.8 Who is allowed to stay sharp
x: The organisational version, and it connects to Chapter 16's economics. Every practice in §19.7 costs time now and preserves capability later. Chapter 17 §17.6 showed the behavioural shifts have a public-good structure — cost borne individually and visibly this sprint, benefit accruing systemically and later. The habits here have the same shape, with an added twist: the benefit accrues partly to the individual and partly to the organisation, on different timescales. An engineer who attempts before delegating is slower this week and more capable next year. Under a throughput mandate — which Chapter 12's seventh prohibition forbids and which the best-documented enterprise case implemented anyway — that engineer is underperforming, measurably, on the metric being watched. So the organisation gets what it measures, and what it measures is Chapter 14's do-not-measure list. The uncomfortable inference: in most organisations today, staying sharp is a private expense that the measurement system penalises. Whoever is best positioned to catch the failures the harness cannot catch — Chapter 8's misdiagnosis, over-engineering, unrequested features, correctness against unstated intent — is the person paying out of pocket to remain able to do it. That is not a mindset problem. It is Chapter 16's Figure 16.1 with a person in place of a team, and the remedy is the same: it must be funded deliberately, or it will not happen.

Offloading degrades verification judgment specifically — the one faculty the lifecycle now leans on hardest and whose feedback signal Chapter 18 showed is disconnected — but the study that identifies the problem also identifies the protective variable, and the order in which you delegate turns out to determine whether the work deposits anything.

Does any of this hold for experienced engineers over months? All three studies are short-horizon, and two use students. The population this book addresses — professionals maintaining production systems over years — has not been measured, and the effect could be larger (more to lose) or smaller (competence already consolidated). Is the ordering effect real for code? The brain-to-LLM finding is from essay writing with 54 participants. Applying it to code review is an inference. It is also nearly free to test, and Chapter 18's prediction log is already the intervention. Are verification and specification judgment genuinely separable? §19.6's resolution depends on it. If specification competence is downstream of verification experience, the resolution fails and Chapter 20's problem generalises to everyone. How long does cognitive debt take to repay? The MIT framing implies recoverability. Nothing establishes the time constant, and it matters enormously for whether periodic unassisted work is a sufficient remedy. Does a better harness accelerate the atrophy? §19.1's paradox says tool-confidence rises with harness maturity. That predicts, uncomfortably, that Level 4 organisations should show more offloading than Level 2 ones. Nobody has looked.

The shifts divide into informational ones, which respond to being told, and behavioural ones, which do not. Everything at stake here is on the second list. METR's cohort knew the result and still felt fast. A workshop transmits information to a faculty that is not the one making the error. There is a deeper reason, and it follows from §20.1. The problem is not that juniors lack knowledge about how to work with agents. It is that the experiences which used to build judgment have been removed from their week. You cannot restore an experience by describing it. The gap is in hours spent being wrong about a real system and finding out, and no curriculum delivers that by exposition. So the framing that follows from the book's own thesis: this is not a training problem, it is a work-allocation problem. Chapter 5's remedy for every withdrawn good was to buy it deliberately. The purchase here is deliberately allocated work whose purpose is learning rather than delivery — which costs delivery, which is why it will not happen by default.

x: Now the hard part, which most writing on this subject omits. The traditional apprenticeship channel was review: a senior reads a junior's work carefully, explains what is wrong, and the explanation is the teaching. It worked because review was already happening and the pedagogy was, again, a by-product. Chapter 3 established that review capacity is the binding constraint. Chapter 16 reported the enterprise measurement: per-reviewer load roughly doubled while per-capita throughput rose 2.09× B. So apprenticeship-by-review now competes directly for the scarcest resource in the organisation, against throughput, at exactly the moment that resource came under maximum pressure. There is no clever resolution. Apprenticeship review and throughput review are different activities and cannot be done with the same hours. A senior reading a junior's change to teach is reading slowly, asking questions whose answers they already know, and explaining. A senior clearing a queue is doing none of that. Which means it has to be separately budgeted, and that is Chapter 16's public-good argument arriving one more level down: the cost is borne by a team this quarter and the benefit accrues to the organisation in three years, to a person who may by then work somewhere else. No team will fund it, and none should be asked to.

Chapter 21 — Anti-Patterns None of these is a mistake. Each is what a competent person does under a pressure this book has already documented. What you'll learn: The four tests an anti-pattern must pass to be content rather than scolding Why every one of the nine is locally rational, and which documented pressure produces it The good practice each one resembles — and the line between them, because over-correction is the second failure The pathology sequence: they are not independent, and the early ones predict the later ones Why most of them are invisible by construction, and the instrument from Parts II–III that detects each The claim this chapter defends: these nine failures are not lapses of discipline. They are the predictable output of the incentive structures established in Chapters 3, 7, 8, and 16 — which means the remedy is never try harder and is always change the thing that makes it rational.

A catalogue of things that are obviously bad teaches nothing. So four tests, in keeping with Chapters 12, 14, 15, and 17. 1. It must be attractive. Nobody adopts a practice that looks like a mistake. A real anti-pattern is the locally rational choice — cheaper, faster, or the only move available under pressure. If it is merely an error, naming it adds nothing. 2. It must have an early warning sign observable before the damage. Otherwise it is a post-mortem category rather than a diagnostic. 3. It must have a specific correction. "Be more careful" is not a correction; it is the absence of one. 4. It must be distinguishable from the good practice it resembles. Every anti-pattern is a degenerate form of something legitimate. Harness Theatre resembles having a harness; Review Collapse resembles review by exception; Agent Washing resembles adoption. If the line is not drawn, readers abandon the good version too — and over-correction is the second failure mode of every anti-pattern catalogue ever written. Test 4 is the one most such lists omit, and it is why each entry below carries a resembles line.

The nine are not independent. They cause each other, in a direction, which makes the early ones predictive. Read the figure as a diagnostic. REVIEW COLLAPSE — approving faster than comprehension allows. Why it is rational. Chapter 3 established four responses to a saturating review queue. Valve 2 is to reduce service time per item, and it is the only valve an individual reviewer controls: they cannot hire, cannot slow arrivals, and cannot install sensors between now and end of day. So they read less. Chapter 16 measured the pressure — per-reviewer load roughly doubled B. Resembles: review by exception, which this book recommends. The line matters more than the anti-pattern: Review by exception is licensed skipping — a blocking sensor covers a class of defect and a drill has shown it fires, so the reviewer is entitled not to look. Review Collapse is unlicensed skipping — the reviewer stops looking without anything having taken over. The behaviour is identical from outside. Only the evidence differs. Early warning. Chapter 14 §14.3's gaming mode: wait time falling while first-pass acceptance rate rises. Faster approvals with fewer objections is capacity relief only if a control was installed; otherwise it is the signature. Detection. Make the skipping licensed. Chapter 13's re-founded A2: a held-out acceptance set the agent never sees, plus blocking sensors in the edit cycle. Then the reviewer's reduced reading is a decision rat

HARNESS THEATRE — an elaborate configuration nobody maintains and no sensor enforces. Why it is rational. Chapter 7 §7.7's cost gradient, operating on harness authors: a paragraph in a context file takes minutes, requires no tooling, breaks nothing, and produces an artefact that looks like progress in a pull request. A wired check costs a quarter and a permanent owner. Both are "harness work". Chapter 15 showed the field's distribution is exactly what that gradient predicts. Resembles: having a harness. Nobody can say why a rule is in the context file. Detection. Chapter 14 §14.6's harness coverage, computed correctly — the proportion of known recurring failure modes with a control that has demonstrably fired in a drill. Without the drill requirement, coverage measures configuration and is itself theatre. Correction. Date every guide with the failure it was added for; drill on a schedule; retire what no longer fires. DEBT BLINDNESS — celebrating month-one velocity while structural metrics climb. Why it is rational. Chapter 4 §4.1: the ledger is asymmetric in measurability before it is asymmetric in outcome. Benefits are prompt, countable, and have an advocate. Costs are deferred, contestable, and owned by nobody. Reasoning from the countable side is not negligence; it is what a manager with a quarterly reporting cycle can actually do. Resembles: appropriate focus on delivery. Early warning. Chapter 14 §14.8: your dashboard mixes horizons. Fast metrics beside slow ones teach every viewer within a month that the slow ones do not matter — they are flat because they are slow, and proximity says otherwise. Detection. Horizon-segregated boards: operational metrics weekly with the team, structural metrics quarterly with a named owner and a standing agenda slot. Correction. BENCHMARK CARGO CULT — selecting a tool on a leaderboard number. Why it is rational. Procurement requires a number. This is the only number on offer, it is public, and it is comparable across vendors. Refusing to use it means deciding without evidence, which is worse in every meeting. Resembles: evidence-based tool selection. Early warning. The number is a level, not a ratio. Chapt

PROMPT-AND-PRAY — generating without any acceptance criterion, where the output matters. Why it is rational. Because it is correct — in its place. Chapter 22 argues at length that this is the right operating point for a prototype, that the research on it is more interesting than the discourse, and that dismissing it is both unfair and useless. The failure is not the practice. It is mode confusion: failing to notice when an artefact stopped being a prototype. Resembles: itself, in a different context. This is the only entry in the catalogue whose good version is the same behaviour, which is why it is the hardest to police and why it gets its own chapter rather than a rule. Early warning. Chapter 23's three crossing signals: the artefact acquired a user, a maintainer, or a secret. Detection and correction. Not "stop prompting". Notice the crossing — and Chapter 23 argues that noticing is the entire problem, because nothing announces it and nobody owns the noticing.

The property that makes this catalogue worth its pages: most of these are invisible from inside the organisation experiencing them. Silence looks like safety. Fast approvals look like efficiency — Chapter 14 showed wait time falls under Review Collapse. A full configuration file looks like maturity. Flat quarterly metrics look like stability. A rising adoption percentage looks like transformation. Each of them presents, to a reasonable observer, as the thing going well. So each needs a detector that does not depend on the failure being visible — and every one already exists in Parts II and III. This is the index: Two observations about that table. The instruments were not designed for this. Drills were introduced in Chapter 8 to answer whether a control still works; autonomy mix in Chapter 14 to show whether delegation is real. That they also detect these failures is a sign the underlying model is coherent rather than a coincidence — a diagnostic system that only detects the failures it was designed around is usually fitted to them. And one entry has no detector, deliberately. Guide Sprawl remains undetectable, and Chapter 14 carries the metric with a null value rather than dropping it, because a catalogue that quietly omits the failure it cannot find is exactly the Silent Sensor at the level of the book.

Part IV asked what delegation does to people, and the answer across five chapters has been more specific than "it changes things." Chapter 17: nine of the ten shifts are one shift seen nine times, and the five that people resist are resisted because they require acting against a signal the nervous system is still producing. Chapter 18: trust is an allocation of verification capacity, and it cannot be calibrated introspectively because the signals have decoupled. Chapter 19: offloading degrades verification judgment specifically, and the order of delegation determines whether work deposits anything. Chapter 20: apprenticeship was a by-product of labour arbitrage, and the group gaining most immediately pays most later. And this chapter: the failures that follow are not moral. They are what competent people do under queue pressure, cost gradients, and measurement asymmetries — every one of which was documented with evidence in Parts I to III before it was named here. That is the argument for why a lifecycle is the right unit of response. You cannot brief someone out of a rational choice. You change the incentive, the measurement, or the capability, and all three are properties of a system rather than of a person. Part V turns to placement and adoption: where the modes belong, when an artefact crosses from one to another, why the codebases that need this most can build it least, what the organisations furthest along have published, and what remains genuinely unsolved.

Every anti-pattern here is the locally rational response to a documented pressure, and most present as the thing going well — so the remedy is never exhortation but a change to the incentive, the measurement, or the capability, and the detector for eight of the nine already exists in this book.

Is the sequence in Figure 21.1 real? It is derived from mechanism rather than observed in organisations. Whether Review Collapse actually predicts Autonomy Creep a quarter later is checkable by anyone with both an incident log and a permissions history. Can Guide Sprawl be detected? The one entry with no instrument. A conflict analysis over layered context files looks tractable and does not exist; Galster's authors and Böckeler both call for it independently. Are there anti-patterns specific to Level 3 and 4 organisations? Every failure here is available at Level 1. A field with almost nobody above Level 1 has not yet generated the pathologies of maturity, and they will not resemble these. Does naming them help? This chapter assumes that a named, mechanism-linked failure mode is easier to resist than an unnamed one. That is a widely held belief about anti-pattern catalogues and I am not aware of evidence for it.

Chapter 13 defined A2 — Delegated: the agent completes a scoped task and the human reviews the resulting diff. Vibe coding has the delegation. The human still verifies. They verify by looking, running it, and judging — live, in the moment, against a standard that exists only in their mind at that moment. This is more precise and it is more useful, because it immediately yields the condition under which the mode is correct rather than merely popular. The acceptance criterion lives in one person's live judgment. So the mode works exactly when that judgment is an adequate acceptance test — and fails, predictably, when it is not. Chapter 23 — The Prototype Crossing The code does not change when it crosses. That is the entire problem. What you'll learn: Why the crossing is invisible to the apparatus we built for noticing change Four signals, each derived from one of Chapter 22's failure conditions rather than listed Why the crossing is a ratchet, and why the value of noticing decays Who owns the noticing — nobody — and why that means it must be mechanised What to do in the first hour after detection, including the option most discussions omit The class of unowned work this book keeps rediscovering, and its category-level remedy The claim this chapter defends: the crossing is a change in an artefact's context, not in the artefact, so version control — our entire infrastructure for noticing change — is blind to it by construction. But all four signals are mechanically detectable from artefacts you already have, which makes this one of the few failures in this book with a cheap and complete instrument.

Chapter 22 established that vibe coding is correct wherever one person's live judgment is an adequate acceptance test, and that it fails when four specific conditions are exceeded. It then noted the property that makes this practically difficult: Nobody moves into mode confusion deliberately. The artefact moves. A weekend prototype acquires a user. A script someone wrote to check something acquires a maintainer. A demo acquires a credential. In each case the mode was correct when it was chosen and became incorrect without anyone making a decision. That is not a discipline failure. It is a detection failure, and the detection failure has a specific structure worth understanding before proposing a remedy.

Five mechanisms, and the first is the one that matters most. The crossing happens to the context, not the code. When your script acquires its first user, nothing in the repository is different. No line changed. No commit. No diff, no pull request, no pipeline run. And our entire apparatus for noticing change — version control, code review, CI — watches the artefact. It is a change of kind wearing a change of degree. One user does not feel different from zero users. But the obligations shift discretely: at one user, someone else can now suffer a loss you will not observe. At two maintainers, intent must be transmitted rather than remembered. At one credential, the artefact becomes worth attacking. Each threshold is genuinely discrete and none of them feels it. Nothing triggers the noticing. No ticket arrives. This is precisely the structure Chapter 4 identified in the missing homeostat and Chapter 12 identified in the outer loop's Observe phase: work with no triggering event loses every prioritisation contest to work that has one. The incentive runs against noticing. Whoever notices inherits the consequence. The author gets asked to harden it; the person who noticed gets told their dependency is unsupported. Noticing is costly to the noticer and beneficial to everyone else, which is a structure this book has now met several times and which §23.7 addresses properly. And the crossing is often invisible to the person who caused it. The engineer who starts calling your script does

The research notes for this book proposed three signals — a user, a maintainer, a secret. Deriving them from Chapter 22's conditions rather than listing them produces a fourth, and the fourth is the most important one for agentic work. Chapter 22 §22.2 established that vibe coding is correct exactly while one person's live judgment is an adequate acceptance test, and gave four ways that fails. Each failure has a corresponding, observable event. The fourth signal deserves emphasis because it is new to the agentic era and because Chapter 13 already named its consequence. A schedule is a crossing because it silently promotes the artefact to A4 — Continuous: running unprompted, without anyone present. Chapter 13 §13.6 established that A4 is legitimately available today only where blast radius is near zero or acceptance is mechanically complete. An artefact that acquires a cron entry has been moved to A4 without anyone assessing whether it qualifies. No permission was granted; a scheduler was configured. This is the most common unexamined promotion in engineering organisations, and it is invisible for the same reason as the rest: adding a schedule is a configuration change somewhere else, not a change to the code.

t: 23.4 A ratchet, and a decaying option
x: Two properties determine how urgently this should be handled. Crossings are one-way. An artefact rarely un-acquires a user. Dependencies accumulate, maintainers arrive, credentials get granted, schedules get set. The state is monotone, so a missed crossing is not a delayed problem — it is a permanent one that grows. The crossing changes an artefact's context rather than the artefact, so every instrument we built for noticing change is blind to it — but all four signals are mechanically detectable from artefacts you already have, which makes this the rare failure with a cheap and complete instrument that nobody has built.

What is the base rate? Nobody knows what fraction of production systems began as prototypes that crossed unnoticed. That matters practically, because it rules out a whole class of hope. Chapter 13 §13.5 scored harnessability on six questions: types enforced, a held-out acceptance set, mechanically enforced boundaries, blocking sensors in the edit cycle, reliable reference enumeration, and drill evidence. Not one of them mentions age. And two counter-examples settle it. A twenty-year-old Java service with strict types, enforced layering, and a comprehensive test suite scores high — and it is thoroughly legacy. A team with a well-structured fifteen-year-old monolith should stop apologising for its age and read its H-score. x: One sequencing claim, and it is not optional. Chapter 10 §10.6 established that whether duplication is debt depends on whether you built the graph: what makes extraction expensive is the fan-in enumeration problem, and lexical search supplies recall without a guarantee. An agent — or an engineer — that finds three of six call sites, extracts, and breaks production has learned something true about its instruments. In a legacy codebase this is not a marginal effect. Without reliable reference enumeration, refactoring is genuinely dangerous, teams correctly refuse to do it, and the codebase's structure cannot improve. The graph is not an optimisation here; it is the precondition that makes structural improvement affordable at all. This inverts the intuitive order. Chapter 25 — Case Studies Two organisations independently built what Parts II and III derive. That is corroboration. It is also survivorship, and the difference matters. What you'll learn: What this chapter cannot do, and why saying so is better than doing it badly The one properly instrumented organisational case that exists, and what it measured OpenAI's harness: enforced layering, custom linters that inject remediation into agent context, and standing drift agents Stripe's: blocking pre-push hooks reported as "the single biggest cost reducer at agent scale" Why the case-study matrix is almost entirely empty, and which cell is missing The reading error that turns these accounts into permission when they are a bill The claim this chapter defends: the published exemplars independently arrived at the structural controls, blocking sensors, and standing drift detection this book derives — which is real corroboration. But they are unrepresentative by construction, the population census shows the field looks nothing like them, and the quadrant that matters most has no published case at all.

The plan for this chapter was to recruit or construct four case studies covering a matrix of organisation types. I can do neither honestly. I cannot recruit, having no access to organisations willing to open their telemetry. And constructing four detailed narratives — even labelled as illustrative — would produce exactly the artefact this book has spent twenty-four chapters warning about: plausible, specific, memorable material that readers will cite as evidence because it is shaped like evidence. Chapter 3 documented how claims mutate as they propagate; a constructed case study is a claim optimised for propagation. So this chapter reports what actually exists, says what grade it is, and marks the gaps. That is less satisfying than four tidy narratives and it is the only version worth printing.

Three kinds of evidence about organisational practice exist, and they answer different questions. The middle tier is the one to be careful with. An organisation that publishes a detailed account of its harness is, necessarily, an organisation that has a harness worth publishing. Nobody writes up the eighteen months in which it did not work. §25.7 returns to this.

Chapter 3 used it for productivity, Chapter 16 for review economics. Read as a case study it is the most complete organisational account in existence. A mid-sized commercial B2B software company, several hundred engineers, described by the researchers as a near-ideal and unusually favourable site: young, AI-forward, permissive, commercial tools with no per-seat caps or token budgets. In June 2025 its CTO set an explicit goal to double engineering productivity through AI adoption over twelve months, naming merged pull requests per engineer per month as the progress metric B. What happened, measured across 802 developers and 196,212 pull requests: Outcome | Result | Per-capita throughput | 21.2 → 44.3 PRs/developer (2.09×) | Company-wide volume | 3.1× | AI-authored share | near zero → ~90% | Token spend among PR authors | ~20× | Per-reviewer load | roughly doubled | Automated review | overtook human review | Average PR size | +37% on adoption, +33% post-mandate | Merge and revert rates | flat | The authors' summary is the finding: an enterprise AI mandate is "a process-redesign problem, not a tooling deployment", and the gain "relocates work downstream rather than removing it." Three things make this the most useful case available, and one makes it limited. The mandate was documented before the outcome. A CTO email with a date and a named metric, then twenty-six months of telemetry. That ordering is what separates a case study from a retrospective narrative. The metric was met

That gap is the chapter's most important finding, and it has a mechanism: survivorship. Organisations publish harness accounts when they have a harness worth publishing. The eighteen months during which it did not work, the attempt abandoned after a reorganisation, the team that installed hooks and removed them because the false positives were intolerable — none of these produce a blog post. Taleb's silent evidence in its standard form: the record consists entirely of survivors, and we infer the odds from them. The reading error these accounts invite is worth naming, because it is the most expensive mistake available in Part V. Stripe's Minions merge a thousand pull requests weekly behind blueprints and sub-second pre-push hooks. The headline in both cases is the autonomy. The reader takes away the number. Chapter 13 §13.6 established that A3 and A4 are reachable today only via near-zero blast radius or mechanically complete acceptance. Stripe's Minions operate inside blueprints where a deterministic pipeline handles everything except reasoning, and cannot push until local checks pass. Enforced layering, validated by structural tests. Custom linters whose messages carry the fix. Blocking checks that run in under a second. Standing agents that scan for drift and open pull requests. Deterministic code doing everything the model does not need to do. Then the autonomy. In that order, because the order is the argument.

Two well-resourced organisations independently built the structural controls, blocking sensors, and standing drift detection this book derives from unrelated evidence — but they published no outcomes, they are survivors, the census shows the field looks nothing like them, and the quadrant most readers occupy has no published case at all.

What does a low-banked success look like? Figure 25.4's empty cell is the most valuable missing case study in the field. A legacy, untyped organisation reaching L2 would be worth more to most readers than either exemplar here. What is the failure rate? Survivorship means we have no denominator. Of organisations that attempted a harness programme, what fraction got one? Nobody knows, and Gartner's forecast that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by end-2027 is the only adjacent estimate C 🟡. Do the exemplars' controls transfer downward? Both accounts come from organisations with unusual engineering depth. Whether sub-second pre-push hooks and Codex-generated custom linters are achievable by a team of eight is an open and very practical question. What did they try that failed? The most useful thing either organisation could publish is the list of controls they built and removed — which is precisely Chapter 15's L3 artefact test, and precisely what nobody publishes.

Chapter 26 — A 90-Day Adoption Plan Ninety days does not buy Level 3. It buys the evidence with which to decide whether to fund it. What you'll learn: The five tests an adoption plan must pass, including the one about permission that most plans assume away Why this plan does not start with a context file, correcting the version in this book's own outline Three stages, each with a gate that is an artefact test rather than a feeling What to stop at each stage — which matters more than what to start The seductive cheaper substitute waiting at each gate, and why the plan must name its own failure modes What ninety days cannot buy, and why the plan ends in a decision rather than a result The claim this chapter defends: the correct sequence is instrument, then constrain, then close the loop — and it is also the sequence that ascends the permission gradient, so a single engineer can start on Monday and nothing above a manager is needed until day 61. Plans that begin with executive sponsorship do not begin.

Ninety-day plans are the sixth-easiest thing in this book to write badly. So, as with Chapters 12, 14, 15, 17, and 21: the standard first. 1. Every gate is falsifiable. Not "the team feels more confident" but an artefact someone can go and look at. Chapter 15's maturity levels each had an artefact test; the gates here are the same instrument applied to a timeline. 2. Sequenced by dependency, not by comfort. The order must be forced. If steps could be permuted without consequence, it is a checklist with dates attached. 3. It says what to stop. Every plan lists additions. The subtractions are what actually free the capacity to do the additions, and Chapter 3 established that capacity is the binding constraint. 4. It does not consume the constraint. A plan that requires substantial review time to execute is competing with the thing it is trying to fix. This rules out most of what a consultancy would propose. 5. It survives the organisation not caring. This is the test most plans fail by assuming it away. Chapter 16 §16.2 showed the harness is a public good — no stream-aligned team will fund it against feature work and none should be asked to. So a plan whose first step requires central funding will not take its first step. The plan must reach value before it needs a budget. Test 5 turns out to determine the entire ordering, and pleasantly, it does not conflict with test 2.

This book's own outline proposed starting with baseline measurement and a single context file. Chapter 15 makes that wrong, and correcting it is the most consequential decision in the chapter. §15.5 argued that the conventional maturity ladder is sorted by cost of adoption rather than dependency: a hook that runs a type checker on every agent edit depends on an agent loop and a type checker, and does not consult AGENTS.md. The dependency does not exist. Which yields the conclusion that Level 1 is "the only level a single team can fully fund and fully capture" and also the only level that unlocks nothing. So a context file is a fine thing to have and a bad thing to start with. It is the most visible move, the cheapest, the one that produces an artefact in a pull request — and it leaves you exactly where you were. The first move is Chapter 15's questions 3 and 4: one blocking check inside the agent's edit cycle, and a trace store. Everything else in ninety days is downstream of those two. Chapter 25 supplies the confirmation. Stripe describes sub-second blocking pre-push hooks as "the single biggest cost reducer at agent scale" D, and Chapter 7 derived the same conclusion from a benchmark ablation two years earlier.

Why measurement first. Chapter 18 established that self-report is invalid as an instrument — METR's cohort was 19% slower and estimated 20% faster after living through it, and the general overestimation runs around forty percentage points A/B. If you change your practice before baselining, you will never know whether it worked, because the only remaining instrument is the one that does not work. Four of Chapter 14's five starter metrics are computable from data you already have. Metric | Source | Effort | Batch size — median lines per merged change | git | hours | Rework rate — % of merged agent code changed within 14 days | git + authorship attribution | a day | W and λ — open→first human review, and arrivals | review timestamps, excluding bot events | a day | Autonomy mix — distribution of merged work across A0–A4 | a level label on merged changes | a week to start labelling | The fifth, time-to-control, needs failure-mode labels, which Chapter 14 conceded is the hard part. Measure it by hand on a sample of twenty incidents. A hand-computed median is enormously more informative than nothing. Then two installations. Trace capture. Chapter 15 §15.6 identified this as the prerequisite no maturity model lists: the outer loop's only inputs are the inner loop's artefacts, so Level 3 is unreachable without it regardless of how many controls exist. It prevents no defect on its own, which is why it loses every prioritisation argument — and why it goes first, before anyone has to arg

An organisation that keeps a throughput mandate running while executing this plan is applying Chapter 3's valve 2 and valve 3 — reviewing less and batching more — with better instrumentation to watch it happen.

The plan will be attacked by the same force that produced the field's distribution, and it is worth naming in advance. Chapter 7 §7.7 identified a cost gradient operating on harness authors: markdown costs an afternoon; a wired check costs a quarter and an owner. Both are "harness work"; one produces a visible artefact immediately. Chapter 16 §16.2 added the economic layer. That gradient will act on this plan, at every gate, offering a cheaper and more visible substitute for the thing the gate actually requires. This is why the gates are phrased as artefact tests with a yes/no. "We improved our documentation" passes no gate here. "A drill produced evidence this control fired" either happened or did not.

The honest close, and it changes what the plan is for. It does not buy Level 3. Chapter 15 priced L3 as a standing role — someone who owns the harness, runs drills, and decides what to retire. That is a rhythm, not a project. Ninety days lets you traverse the outer loop once, which demonstrates the loop is possible in your organisation. It does not establish it. And Chapter 15 §15.7 warned specifically: "L3 funded as a project decays back to L2 with a larger pile of controls than it started with." A ninety-day programme that ends without a funding decision produces exactly that. So the plan's output is not a capability. It is evidence with which to make a funding argument — which is the argument Chapter 16 said must be made centrally, because the harness is a public good and no stream team will fund it. By day 90 you have what that argument requires: a baseline and a re-measurement on four metrics; demonstrated blocking sensors with drill evidence; one class of work with real acceptance criteria; one traversal of the steering loop with a control installed and a control retired; and a crossing scan telling you what is already in production unowned. And one adjustment by starting position, from Chapter 24 §24.8. This plan is written for the common case — low harnessability, whatever the age of the code. If your H-score is already high, days 1–60 will be faster and the constraint is organisational rather than technical, so start at §26.5 and at Chapter 16. If your codebase is ne

Instrument, then constrain, then close the loop once — a sequence that is forced by dependency and happens also to ascend the permission gradient, so it starts on Monday with one engineer and ends on day 90 not with a capability but with the evidence required to fund one.

Is ninety days the right window? It is long enough to traverse the outer loop once and short enough to hold attention. Whether a single traversal predicts sustained practice is unmeasured, and it is the assumption the whole plan rests on. Does the permission gradient hold in regulated organisations? §26.3's claim that nothing above a manager is needed until day 61 assumes an engineer can wire a hook and store traces without review. In some environments the day-1 move requires a change-control process, which inverts the ordering. What is the drop-out point? Chapter 25 §25.7 noted we have no denominator for harness programmes — survivorship means the failures are unpublished. If most attempts stop, knowing where would be worth more than this plan. Does starting with sensors rather than a context file actually work better? §26.2 corrects the plan on the strength of Chapter 15's dependency argument, which is mechanism rather than evidence. Two teams, ninety days, opposite orderings would settle it.
