Chapter 27 — Open Problems: An Invitation A book that ends with answers has usually stopped looking. What you'll learn: Why "open problem" conflates four different things, and why the distinction determines who can solve each The keystone: one unsolved problem that gates most of Part III Four missing instruments, four missing experiments, and three missing measurements — each stated precisely enough to start on What this book probably got wrong, including the argument I would attack first What remains true regardless of how any of it is settled The claim this chapter defends: most of what this field calls unsolved is not unsolved. It is unmeasured, uninstrumented, or untested — three conditions with known remedies and identifiable owners. Exactly one problem here is genuinely hard, and almost everything in Part III is waiting on it.

Every chapter in this book closed with open questions. Collected, they number several dozen, and a list of several dozen is not an invitation — it is a shrug. So four criteria for what earns a place here. Something depends on it. Not curiosity. A decision a practitioner must make, or an argument this book makes, rests on the answer. It is tractable. Stated precisely enough that a competent person could begin on Monday and know what would count as progress. It is unclaimed. Not "someone is probably working on this." And solving it would change what practitioners do, not only what researchers know. That leaves the problems below, and one observation about them that I did not expect when I started assembling this chapter.

"Open problem" is used to cover four situations that differ in the only way that matters — who can address them and with what. That distribution is the chapter's first finding. The discourse treats agentic engineering as a frontier of hard unknowns. The reality is that one problem is hard and the rest are unbuilt, unrun, or uncollected — which is a far more optimistic position than the field's tone suggests, and a far more embarrassing one.

The one genuinely unsolved problem, and the one Part III is waiting on. The question. How do you verify, mechanically, that generated software does what was actually wanted? Why it is hard. Chapter 8 §8.7 stated the circularity precisely: code and tests generated from one model of intent prove consistency, not correctness. Their agreement is evidence about the generator's self-consistency and silent about whether its model of intent matched yours. Böckeler's assessment stands — current practice "puts a lot of faith into the AI-generated tests, that's not good enough yet." What depends on it. More than any other item here. What would count as progress. Not a solution — a bound. Chapter 8 §8.8's held-out acceptance set does not solve the problem; it converts an unbounded exposure into a bounded one. You remain exposed to what you failed to articulate, and no longer to what the generator failed to infer. Progress looks like more of that: mechanisms that shrink the unarticulated residue. The most promising direction, and its limit. Chapter 1 §1.6 noted that Meaning A solved a version of this — nobody building an agent as a product lets the system under test author its acceptance criteria; the eval set is built first, by humans, from stakeholder-aligned success metrics. Chapter 8 attempted the transplant. What did not transfer is the statistical logic: an eval set samples a distribution of user requests, while a feature has a particular intent. Chapter 0 closed with a claim, and it is the right place to end. A harness cannot verify correctness against a requirement that was never articulated. Specification is the last human monopoly. Twenty-seven chapters later, that sentence has survived everything built on top of it, and §27.3 explains why: the one genuinely unsolved problem in this book is precisely the problem of verifying intent. Every control in Parts II and III operates on stated intent. Where intent is unstated, no apparatus helps, and the failure is silent — because generated code that satisfies an unstated requirement incorrectly is indistinguishable from generated code that satisfies it correctly. So the book ends approximately where it began, with the human obligation intact and the machinery around it incomplete. That is not a disappointing conclusion. It is the useful one, because it tells you where to stand. Three things are settled well enough to act on, whatever happens to the rest. The bottleneck moved. Generation is elastic; verification is not. Nothing in the evidence contradicts this, and the best-documented enterprise case doubled throughput while doubling per-reviewer load. Any strategy that increases generation without increasing verification capacity relocates a bottleneck rather than removing one. The controls that used to be free must now be bought. Appendix A — AGENTS.md Reference Patterns Most context files are full of the wrong content. Not badly written — wrong category. Use this appendix to: audit an existing context file, decide what belongs in it, and layer multiple files without creating contradictions nobody can detect. Established in: Chapter 6 (the budget), Chapter 7 (the quadrant), Chapter 9 §9.5 (the division of labour), Chapter 8 §8.9 (contradictions), Chapter 21 (Guide Sprawl).

t: A.1 What belongs here, and what does not
x: Chapter 9 §9.5 established the division of labour that governs everything else in this appendix. A study of 328 CLAUDE.md files found that architectural concerns dominate their content, followed by development guidelines, project overviews, and testing B 🔴. And architecture is a structural property of the code — derivable, mechanically, and kept fresh by a pipeline rather than by hand. Content | Belongs in | Because | Where things are; what calls what; module boundaries; type contracts; what tests cover what | The graph (Ch 9) | Derivable, therefore durable. A hand-written version drifts silently and reads authoritative while wrong | Why it is like this; which debt is deliberate; which convention is load-bearing; what the team is trying to achieve; when not to delegate | The context file | Not derivable at any price. Chapter 5 established it cannot be recovered by interrogating an author | So the test for every line in a context file: Could a machine derive this from the code? If yes, it does not belong here — it belongs in the graph, or it is already checkable by a sensor. If no, it is exactly what this file is for. Chapter 6 gives the second test, from the context budget: the marginal token can be negative, so add a line only if it is more relevant than the average of what is already there. That bar rises as the file improves, which is why the first few lines help enormously and later ones often do not.

Run this on an existing file before adding anything. Most teams delete 40–60% on a first pass. Category 3 is the one people resist deleting, and Chapter 2 is the reason to: a rule compensating for a model deficit that three generations have since closed is not neutral. It consumes the scarce budget, and worse, it teaches every reader that the file's contents are decorative.

Annotated. Each of these records something underivable. The deliberate trade-off. Records a decision an agent would otherwise reverse, with the incident that motivated it. Chapter 4's cost gradient predicts an agent will keep trying to fix this; the note is what stops it. The load-bearing convention. The parenthetical is the valuable half. Chapter 5 established that agents cannot distinguish deliberate convention from habit; this states the distinction explicitly and bounds it. The non-goal. ⚠️ These are guides, so they are belief-based (Chapter 11). They inform; they do not enforce. If the consequence is severe, revoke the capability instead — no write access to migrations/, no network egress for package installs. A sentence here is a reminder, not a control. The escalation instruction. Chapter 14's escalation quality metric depends on the agent knowing when to stop. This is one of the few things a context file does that nothing else can. The pointer, not the payload. Chapter 6's progressive disclosure. Three lines replacing three pages, and unlike the three pages it cannot go stale.

Chapter 7 found 4,768 context files across 2,586 repositories, with CLAUDE.md pointing to AGENTS.md in 301 cases A. Layering is normal. Layering plus no removal plus no detector is Chapter 21's Guide Sprawl. Galster's authors draw the practical implication, and it is the right one: Two rules that prevent the failure: Substantive content lives in exactly one file. If a statement appears in two files it will eventually appear differently in two files, and nothing will tell you. Never let the agent resolve a contradiction. Chapter 8 §8.9: delegating that means accepting a silent, unlogged, per-invocation decision about which of your stated intentions wins. A contradiction is a defect in the harness and belongs to whoever owns it. And the honest gap, from Chapter 21 and Chapter 27: there is no contradiction detector. Both Galster's authors and Böckeler name this independently as a missing tool. Until one exists, the single-source discipline above is the only defence, and it is a convention rather than a control.

Five, each traceable to a chapter. 1. Every guide carries a date and the failure it was added for. Chapter 12's fourth prohibition. Undated guides cannot be pruned, so they accumulate. A one-line HTML comment is enough: 2. Edit, never regenerate. Chapter 6 §6.7: contexts collapse. Repeated wholesale rewriting degrades toward genericity, dropping exactly the specific, hard-won detail that looks like noise to a summariser. A regenerated AGENTS.md will read better and will have quietly deleted the three lines doing all the work. 3. Prune on a schedule. If nothing is ever removed, dilution is where you end up by default. 4. Do not use this file to enforce anything that matters. Chapter 11: guides are belief-based and defeated by injection. Chapter 10 §10.7's ordering — make it impossible, then detect it deterministically, then judge it, then assert it. This file is tier four. 5. Measure whether it is working. Chapter 14's context efficiency — tokens per accepted change — moves in the right direction when a context file is well curated. It is the only feedback available on a file whose failures are otherwise silent.

Everything above, applied. This is what a good context file looks like: short, underivable, dated. Roughly forty lines. Chapter 7's evidence says the median repository has one or two context files and little else; the goal is not to make this file bigger but to make every line in it underivable.

x: A template is not a pile of files; it is a bundle with an owner and a contract. t: B.7 What this kit does not do
x: Three limits, stated so the kit is not oversold. It does not verify behaviour. Chapter 8's unsolved third. Every sensor here checks maintainability or architecture fitness. Whether the software does what was actually wanted is what the held-out acceptance set bounds and does not solve. It may not survive a model migration. Appendix C — Autonomy Policy Template An autonomy level enforced by instruction is not an autonomy level. It is a hope with a number attached. Use this appendix to: write the artefact that makes an autonomy decision auditable — the thing Chapter 11 §11.9 argued accountability should attach to, instead of to an individual approval. Established in: Chapter 13 (the ladder, the scoring instrument, revocations), Chapter 11 §11.9 (accountability), Chapter 16 §16.3 (the named owner), Chapter 21 (Autonomy Creep).

Chapter 11 established that accountability once travelled with authorship. Authorship is now machine, so responsibility defaults to approval — precisely the gate Chapter 5 showed had collapsed. The result is that responsibility sits on the weakest remaining signal. The way out is to attach accountability to the decision that actually determines outcomes: this class of change may run at this level of authority. That decision has to exist as a document for anyone to be accountable for it. Three properties make it real rather than decorative: It is per class of work, not per team. The same agent may run at A4 on dependency bumps and A0 on the payment path, in the same repository, in the same hour. Every level is implemented as revoked capabilities. Chapter 13 §13.3. If the boundary lives in a context file, it is a belief-based control and Chapter 11 showed what those are worth under injection — or under ordinary misunderstanding. The downgrade trigger is written while everyone is calm. Chapter 13 §13.9: a level granted with no stated conditions for revocation will never be revoked, because after an incident the conversation is about the incident rather than about whether the grant was sound.
Copy, fill, commit next to the code it governs. One file per class of work, or one file with a section per class.
Filled in, for the two classes most organisations should write first — because they sit at opposite ends and make the instrument's point.

The dependency bot has a schedule, which silently promoted it to A4 without anyone assessing whether it qualified. Either reduce B4 (pin, stage, canary) to reach blast 0, or drop the schedule.

t: Class: changes to the payment path
x: Note what this shows. Harnessability is excellent — this is the best-instrumented code in the organisation. And the ceiling is still A0/A1, because blast radius vetoes (Chapter 13 §13.4). No amount of harness quality makes a severe-blast-radius change eligible for autonomy; you reduce the blast radius instead, or you accept the ceiling. Together the two examples make the instrument's real payoff visible, and it is the one Chapter 13 §13.5 predicted: a uniform "A2 everywhere" policy is simultaneously above ceiling on the payment path and below it on dependency updates. The gain from scoring is not speed — it is reallocation of the scarce resource.

Four failure modes, each from Chapter 21, each with its early sign. The policy is written and the capabilities are not revoked. §5 is empty or aspirational. Early sign: you cannot name the mechanism in the "how it is enforced" column. This is the most common failure and it makes the whole document decorative. No downgrade trigger. §6 left blank because nothing had gone wrong yet. Early sign: the review date passes and the policy is renewed without discussion. Scope ambiguity. §1 says "backend changes". Early sign: two people disagree about whether a change is in this class, and resolve it in favour of the higher level. This is Autonomy Creep's entry point. Nobody executes. §6's triggers fire and nothing happens because the named person moved teams. Early sign: the owner field has not been updated in two reorganisations. Test it the way Chapter 13 §13.9 prescribes: attempt to exceed the level. Ask an A2 agent to merge. If it can, you are not at A2, whatever this document says — and that is the only verification that means anything.

Appendix D — Metrics Instrumentation Guide Report the horizon with the metric, or the metric is not a claim. Use this appendix to: actually collect what Chapter 14 defines — with the definitional choices that decide whether each number means anything, and the caveats that keep it honest. Established in: Chapter 14 (definitions, guardrails, gaming modes), Chapter 12 §12.8 (artefacts are the prerequisite), Chapter 26 §26.3 (four are computable from git).

Chapter 12 §12.8 stated it without hedging: a lifecycle without artefacts has no outer loop. Not a weak one — none. Every metric below except batch size depends on capturing something that is not captured by default. Authorship attribution deserves a note because it is easy and everyone skips it. The enterprise study used a repository-level convention — an internal created-by-ai label applied at PR creation — plus bot identity detection and Co-authored-by trailers B. Any of the three works. Without one, rework rate and autonomy mix are uncomputable.

Median lines per merged change. Free — you already have the data. This is not a health metric. It is the unit-stability guard for every count in this guide, and Chapter 14 §14.4 explains why: enlarging batches leaves utilisation exactly unchanged while degrading reviewability, blast radius per item, and revert granularity. The enterprise study measured PR size rising ~37% on adoption and a further ~33% post-mandate B. Report it beside every count metric. A throughput number without a batch-size number beside it is not a claim.

The constraint itself. Chapter 14 §14.3. The definitional choice that decides everything: Excluding automated review events is essential and not optional. The enterprise study found bots at roughly 38% of review events and half of all comments, and set its own boundary at the first human review for exactly this reason B. Count a review event as human if the actor is not in your bot identity list and the comment is not templated. You never need to estimate μ, which is the point: reviewer capacity is not headcount × hours, it is the rate at which reviews complete at adequate quality, and adequate quality is precisely what degrades silently under load. ⚠️ Pair W with a scrutiny proxy — human review comments per unit of change, or first-pass acceptance rate. W falling while acceptance rate rises is not capacity relief; it is Chapter 21's Review Collapse. ⚠️ The bands are reasoned, not fitted. Chapter 14 flags this as an open question: anyone with two years of review telemetry could calibrate them properly in an afternoon.

Median elapsed time from a failure mode's second occurrence to a control that prevents it. The outer loop's own clock. This is the hard one, and Chapter 14 said so. It requires classifying failures into modes across sessions, which Chapter 27 lists as the single most enabling missing instrument in the field. What to do until that exists: measure it by hand on a sample of twenty incidents. Tag each with a coarse failure mode, find the second occurrence, find the control. A hand-computed median from twenty incidents is enormously more informative than nothing, and it is the only way to test Chapter 12 §12.7's uncomfortable claim — that a monthly outer loop cannot regulate an inner loop running dozens of times a day. Read it as: a median measured in quarters means the steering loop is a historian. A median measured in weeks means it is a regulator.
Add these once drills are running (Appendix B.5). Before that, harness coverage measures configuration and is itself Harness Theatre.

The denominator is known failure modes — the ones you have already met. It is silent about everything you have not encountered, and it can read 100% while you are fully exposed to a class of failure nobody has imagined. Per sensor: how often it fires, and what share of firings were real. | | Source | Sensor outcome logs | Window | 90 days | Decision | Which sensors to retire, fix, or promote from advisory to blocking | Gaming mode | Tuning a noisy sensor to silence rather than to accuracy | A sensor with zero firings in 90 days is a drill candidate, not a success.

Currently unmeasurable. Chapter 14 carries it deliberately with a null value, because a metric with no detector is a standing statement about a missing tool rather than a missing discipline. Both Galster's authors and Böckeler name it independently as a gap. Report it as "no detector exists" rather than dropping the row.

The denominator is deliberate: a change merged and then reworked is not accepted, it is deferred. ⚠️ Human review minutes are the dominant term and the hardest to instrument. Chapter 16 §16.6's finding is that organisations meter the abundant input (tokens) carefully and the scarce one (review minutes) not at all. If you exclude review minutes because they are hard, you have measured the cheap part and called it the cost. Approximation that is better than omission: (number of reviewers × median time-in-review-tool per change). Weak, gameable, and vastly better than a zero.

t: Review load per engineer per week
x: Hours spent reviewing, per person. Chapter 3's true capacity constraint; the enterprise study measured it roughly doubling B. ⚠️ Do not collect this by asking. Chapter 18 disqualified self-report. Derive it from review event timestamps, and accept that the number is a lower bound. ⚠️ Never put this in a performance review. The moment it becomes a performance measure it becomes worthless, and it will also penalise exactly the apprenticeship review Chapter 20 §20.7 says is being squeezed out.

Tokens consumed per accepted change. Chapter 6's budget made measurable. It moves in the right direction for two different good reasons — better payload curation, and graph traversal replacing exploratory search. LocAgent reported an ≈86% cost reduction from that substitution B. ⚠️ Hold the model constant or normalise. Otherwise the metric measures your procurement decisions.

Complexity trend, duplication trend, batch size. Chapter 4 §4.7: "track these as guardrail metrics, not vanity metrics" — you do not optimise them, you watch the shape of the curve. Each needs a threshold and an owner, or it is a chart. The threshold need not be principled: If duplication rises for two consecutive quarters, the platform team opens an investigation. That is a perfectly good rule and vastly better than watching.
